abstract: Geo-foundation models (GFMs) are typically evaluated by downstream task predictive performance, revealing little about which physical features they are sensitive to or use in prediction. This limits developers' ability to test hypotheses about model behaviour and users' ability to select models for new tasks. We propose Physics-Informed Concept Probing (PiCo), a post-hoc framework for explaining GFM predictions. PiCo identifies concept vectors in a GFM's embedding space by generating synthetic multispectral satellite observations from a 3D radiative transfer model coupled with a game engine. These vectors reveal physical sensitivities that inform domain-based hypotheses about downstream performance. Projecting embeddings onto these concept vectors produces low-dimensional representations for quantifying concept importance in making predictions. We evaluate PiCo on three GFMs with different input modalities using seven physical concepts covering forest leaf optics and canopy structure. In ground-cover estimation, RGB restriction reduces dry-matter sensitivity and disproportionately degrades predictions for dry vegetation and bare ground, supporting a hypothesis derived from sensitivity analysis. For hierarchical forest type and tree species classification, concept representations retain 70.0-93.8% of full-embedding accuracy. Models capture similar physical contrasts between classes, such as structural differences between broadleaf forest and cleared ground and leaf-water-content differences between oak and beech, yet differ in the strength of these contrasts and the concepts driving classification. PiCo thus provides a physical basis for hypothesis testing and model assessment, with potential applicability beyond Earth observation wherever forward models enable controlled simulation and pretrained embeddings are accessible for probing.

title: Separating mixtures of single-fiber orientation distributions for increased sensitivity to crossing white matter fibers
abstract: Intro: Diffusion MRI allows for in vivo probing of brain tissue architecture via micron-level diffusion aggregated at the millimeter scale, but crossing white matter fibers decrease the sensitivity of downstream tasks such as microstructural modeling and tractography. Current fixel-based methods for identifying the number, orientation, and spread of fibers rely on finding the peaks of fiber orientation distributions from constrained spherical deconvolution. However, this method is biased by the spreads of nearby fibers and fails at angular separations lower than approximately 40-50 degrees. Methods: In this work, we perform a constrained nonlinear optimization called fiber segmentation by signal splitting and iterative least squares estimation (FISSILE), modeling each voxel as a mixture of single-fiber distributions. We use FISSILE to fit axially symmetric fibers in simulations and on three in vivo human subjects from the Human Connectome Project, an ex vivo raccoon brain, as well as the same human subject scanned twice at two different signal-to-noise ratios (SNRs). Results: On simulated data, FISSILE successfully identifies fibers at an angular separation of 40° and a volume fraction of 0.1 at an SNR as low as 30, while MRtrix3's fod2fixel is limited to 60° separation and 0.1 volume fraction at the same SNR. On acquired data, FISSILE identified 85.8% of white matter voxels on average in human brains and 79.4% in the raccoon with at least one fiber crossing, whereas fod2fixel identified 30.1% and 44.5%. The number of white matter fiber crossings was mildly sensitive to different noise levels in the human subject with two acquisitions. Conclusion: A method that models the crossing fiber phenomenon as an unmixing problem increases sensitivity to individual fibers for more precise characterization of anatomy.

title: The Sill distribution for all partial waves
abstract: In high-energy physics, short-lived resonances appearing in scattering processes are described by energy-dependent spectral functions. The relativistic Breit--Wigner distribution (rBW), obtained as a relativistic extension of the standard Breit--Wigner form, is commonly employed owing to its simplicity. However, when the lower-energy threshold lies sufficiently close to the resonance peak, sizable deviations from the rBW line shape are expected. The Sill distribution provides a simple way to incorporate the physical threshold while preserving exact normalization, but in its original formulation it is inherently restricted to $s$-wave decays. Here, we extend the Sill distribution to arbitrary partial waves. The correct $\ell$-wave threshold behaviour is implemented while exact normalization is retained through a simple modification of the mass term of the propagator. As a benchmark, the $p$-wave Sill provides a very good description of the $Δ(1232)^{++}$ line shape up to 1.35 GeV and simultaneously reproduces its on-shell mass and width and its complex pole position, in agreement with independent determinations compiled by the PDG.

title: Chemotaxis models with signal-dependent sensitivity and a logistic-type source, III: Bifurcation and spike-like solutions
abstract: This third paper in a series on a parabolic-elliptic chemotaxis model studies bifurcation of positive constant equilibria in one space dimension. We consider $$ \left\{ \begin{array}{ll} u_t=Δu-χ_0\nabla\cdot\left(\frac{u^m}{(1+v)^β}\nabla v\right)+au-bu^{1+α}, & x\inΩ,\\ 0=Δv-μv+νu^γ, & x\inΩ,\\ \frac{\partial u}{\partial n}=\frac{\partial v}{\partial n}=0, & x\in\partialΩ, \end{array} \right. $$ where $Ω$ is a bounded interval, $α,γ,m,μ,ν>0$, $χ_0\in\mathbb R$, and $a,b,β\ge0$. Building on earlier results on global existence, boundedness, persistence, and stabilization, we take $χ_0$ as the bifurcation parameter and examine the effects of $β$ and the domain size on the bifurcation. Center manifold reduction yields a coefficient $β_{n_0}$ at a simple bifurcation mode $n_0$ of a positive constant equilibrium. The pitchfork bifurcation is supercritical if $β_{n_0}>0$ and subcritical if $β_{n_0}<0$. Stronger desensitization raises the sensitivity required for loss of linear stability. Bifurcation may be supercritical for small $β$ but is always subcritical for sufficiently large $β$. Thus, desensitization makes patterns harder to trigger and favors abrupt rather than continuous emergence. The bifurcation mode increases with domain size, allowing more complex spatial patterns. Under suitable conditions, we prove unbounded continuation of local bifurcation branches. We also show that large-sensitivity stationary sequences satisfying a peak-gap hypothesis develop spike-like profiles. Numerical continuation and time-evolution experiments illustrate the bifurcating branches and spike-like solutions and suggest unbounded continuation and increasingly sharp stationary profiles.

title: Disentangling geometry & growth in cosmic neutrino mass constraints: a more physical split and diagnostic
abstract: Recent cosmological data hint at a neutrino mass sum below the minimum value allowed by the neutrino mass oscillation experiments, with a preference for the opposite of massive neutrinos ("negative" neutrino masses). Since massive neutrinos impact the expansion history of the Universe, which in turn modifies the growth of structure, we ask whether such a preference originates from the observed geometry or structure growth, and whether the two agree. In this paper, we introduce a more physical split of $\sum m_ν$ into parameters $\sum m_ν^{geo}$ and $\sum m_ν^{growth}$ based on their physical effects, with extension to negative values. We split the expansion rate at the Boltzmann-code level: $\sum m_ν^{geo}$ sets $H(z)$ for distance computation, and $\sum m_ν^{growth}$ sets $H(z)$ for perturbation evolution. Combining Planck primary CMB, Planck+ACT+SPT CMB lensing and DESI BAO data, we find similar sensitivity and "negative" preference from geometry and growth with $\sum m_ν^{geo} = -0.07\pm0.10$ eV (68% C.L.) and $\sum m_ν^{growth} = -0.13^{+0.10}_{-0.12}$ eV (68% C.L.). The difference of the two is a null test of the $Λ$CDM model, passed by current data at $0.4σ$ level. Forecasts on Advanced SO CMB and DESI DR3 BAO show that $0.058$ eV would be rejected at $3.0σ$ from the geometry channel alone, if the negative mean of $\sum m_ν^{geo} = -0.07$ eV persists. The two channels can also provide a powerful new diagnostic between possible origins of the neutrino mass tension. With future CMB and BAO data, our Fisher forecasts show that an incorrect dark energy model displaces $\sum m_ν^{geo}$ from $0.058$ eV by $3.1$-$4.2σ$ and $\sum m_ν^{growth}$ by $1.1$-$1.3σ$, while an underestimated reionization optical depth reverses the pattern, $2.7$-$3.6σ$ in $\sum m_ν^{growth}$ against at most $0.23σ$ in $\sum m_ν^{geo}$. (Abridged)

title: A differentiable PCA-GPR surrogate framework for full-transient Bayesian inverse uncertainty quantification of black-box nuclear thermal-hydraulic systems
abstract: Complex transient energy systems require uncertainty-quantified predictions, but Bayesian inverse uncertainty quantification (IUQ) is often impractical because posterior sampling with high-fidelity system codes requires many expensive full-transient simulations. This study develops a surrogate-assisted Bayesian IUQ framework that makes full-time-series calibration practical for the NACIE heavy-liquid-metal natural-circulation loop. The key innovation is to transform a black-box transient simulator into a differentiable probabilistic emulator by combining principal component analysis with Gaussian process regression (PCA--GPR). The surrogate reconstructs complete multichannel temperature and mass-flow histories from a compact latent representation, preserving dominant temporal and cross-channel correlations while enabling automatic differentiation of the log posterior. This allows both gradient-free ensemble slice sampling and gradient-informed sampling with the No-U-Turn Sampler and Microcanonical Langevin Monte Carlo. Five principal components capture more than 99\% of the output variance, and the surrogate achieves normalized root-mean-square errors below 2\%. Compared with direct Flownex SE evaluations, the surrogate reduces likelihood-evaluation cost by approximately 3000-fold while preserving posterior statistics and correlations. Posterior predictive analyses show reduced bias, narrower intervals, and improved agreement with measurements and independent validation.

title: Two-Stage Score Estimation for Group-Specific Diffusion Models
abstract: Generative modeling across related distributions raises a question: how can shared structure support accurate generation for a target distribution with limited observations? We develop a statistical framework for diffusion transfer that analyzes a shared pooled score together with a target-specific offset. Under Besov regularity of the pooled density and a stable hierarchical composition model for the offset, we derive convergence rates that separate the costs of learning these components and identify when a simpler offset yields a faster risk-bound rate than separate fitting. Under suitable boundary and regularity assumptions, we prove that the offset remains bounded and jointly regular as diffusion time approaches zero. These results allow the lower time cutoff to vanish polynomially and provide total-variation guarantees for diffusion models as density estimators. Synthetic simulations and image benchmarks provide a proof of concept for the framework.

title: How to Train Your Little Dragon: Teaching a Small Language Model to Construct and Refine GPU Optimization Scripts
abstract: Compiler transformations interact, making GPU kernel optimization a search for combinations that preserve the computation while improving performance. We introduce HOW TO TRAIN YOUR LITTLE DRAGON, a training method that teaches a small language model both to construct complete optimization scripts and to improve existing ones. Instead of ranking candidates or generating kernel code, our model generates optimization scripts. We devise a compact, lossless representation whose deterministic decoding reconstructs the exact compiler trace, preserving its transformation parameters and dependencies. We use a compiler framework TVM MetaSchedule to build training data on 54,116 distinct workloads, and construct 108,594 examples in two training sets: 60,236 teach the model to generate an optimized script from an unoptimized kernel, while 48,358 teach it to produce a better script given the kernel and a somewhat optimized script. Supervised fine-tuning teaches the model to construct and improve optimization scripts from these search-derived examples. We then add reinforcement learning with a shaped reward that combines correctness with measured performance, awarding a latency-based bonus only to numerically correct kernels. We apply this training method to a model with 8 billion parameters. After supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning, the model achieves per-attempt correctness of 91.27% for construction and 92.01% for refinement, while reinforcement learning produces faster kernels than supervised training on 88 of 102 construction tasks and 145 of 170 refinement prompts. With only 8B parameters, our LITTLE DRAGON achieves higher per-attempt correctness and better kernel performance than six frontier LLMs: GPT-6 Astra, Opus 5, Kimi-K3, and GLM-5.3 among them, each with hundreds of billions to trillions of parameters, for which task-specific training is unavailable or expensive.

title: Cyclotron: A Recurrence Language for Expressing Interprocessor Communication
abstract: We present Cyclotron, a compiler that expresses streaming dataflow algorithms using recurrence equations, which are then compiled to distributed topologies of interlinked processors. Our compiler lowers a language of recurrences over logical iteration spaces into per-processor programs of sends, receives, and computations. In these recurrences, data accesses are not limited to external accesses to memory; data can live separately on the iteration space itself, allowing internal points to communicate values directly with other points. Users specify this communication directly in the recurrence language, which allows them to express various communication patterns such as a nearest-neighbor systolic exchange, a one-to-all broadcast, a bidirectional split ring, or an asymmetric and piecewise broadcast pattern, which are often not supported by standard distributed linear algebra libraries. These recurrences describe the algorithm and communication independently of how they map onto the hardware. A programmer then chooses which dimensions execute across processors and which execute over time, without rewriting the entire program. Users only specify data dependencies across the iteration space, and the compiler safely generates a program, per process, with correct placement of both communication and computational operators according to the chosen space--time mapping. We evaluate distributed matrix multiplication, TRSM, Cholesky, and fused Cholesky--TRSM on up to 16 CPU nodes and 16 GPUs, comparing against ScaLAPACK, SLATE, and cuSolverMp. Cyclotron is competitive with and often outperforms these hand-optimized libraries; for Cholesky, the best communication strategy changes with problem size and architecture.

title: The Blume-Capel Model as a $ϕ^6$ Field Theory: A Monte Carlo and Flow Model Study
abstract: We report Monte Carlo simulations of a continuous spin variant of the Blume-Capel model. We compute the phase diagrams in the crystal-field-temperature plane, as a function of the softness of the spins. We show that normalizing flows, a class of generative models capable of direct sampling without autocorrelation, are effective samplers across the phase diagram, including in the first-order transition region and in the vicinity of the tricritical point. Finite-size scaling analyses of flow samples locate the first- and second-order transitions as well as the tricritical point with accuracy comparable to canonical and extended-ensemble Monte Carlo.

title: Near-Linear Preprocessing for Range Weighted Longest Increasing Subsequence Queries
abstract: We give a deterministic data structure for range weighted longest increasing subsequence (LIS) queries on $n$ values with positive weights. Preprocessing takes $O(n\log^2 n)$ time and space. Value queries take $O(\log n)$ time, and an optimal subsequence of $k$ elements can be reported in $O(k + \log n)$ time. This resolves an open question on truly subquadratic preprocessing with polylogarithmic query time. The key is a single-crossing property of envelopes for value-separated endpoint sets, enabling $O(\log n)$-time persistent merges. The bounds assume constant-time exact addition and comparison of weights.

title: Competitive displacement in the grass-bushes-trees process on a scale-free network
abstract: The grass-bushes-trees process is a two-type contact process in which the types face asymmetric birth mechanisms. Vertices of a graph can either be occupied by a tree, occupied by a bush, or empty (containing grass). The trees die with rate $1$ and give birth with rate $λ_{\mathcal T}$ on any neighbouring vertex (possibly taking the place of a bush). Bushes die with rate $1$ and give birth with rate $λ_{\mathcal B}$ on any empty neighbouring vertex; in particular, they are forbidden from taking the place of trees. We study this process on a power law random graph, namely the erased configuration model. We study which graph parameters lead to the possibility of coexistence versus the necessity of competitive displacement, i.e. joint metastability or fast extinction of the bushes.

title: EPRV Asteroseismology of the K dwarfs GJ 570 A and GJ 783 A with ESPRESSO. Empirical mode-amplitude scaling in tension with 3D convection simulations
authors: M. J. P. F. G. Monteiro
abstract: Solar-like oscillations in K dwarfs have intrinsically low amplitudes, making them challenging to detect in space-based photometry. The advent of Extremely Precise Radial Velocity (EPRV) instrumentation enables Doppler asteroseismology in the mid-K regime, providing a new opportunity to test mode-excitation and damping physics. We investigate the scaling of oscillation amplitudes with stellar parameters and assess whether 3D surface convection simulations reproduce the observed amplitude behavior. High-cadence ESPRESSO radial-velocity time series were obtained over five and six consecutive nights for the K dwarfs GJ 570 A (K4 V) and GJ 783 A (K2.5 V), respectively. We identified oscillation modes from weighted power spectra and extracted them via sine-wave fitting following spectral deconvolution. Peak mode amplitudes were measured from heavily smoothed power spectra. For comparison, we performed 3D radiative-hydrodynamical simulations including excitation and damping-rate calculations. We measured 6 modes for GJ 570 A and 24 for GJ 783 A ($\ell=0$-$2$, and $\ell=3$ for GJ 783 A). The peak radial-mode amplitudes are $2.57 \pm 0.52\:{\rm cm\,s^{-1}}$ and $4.90 \pm 0.81\:{\rm cm\,s^{-1}}$, respectively. These results support a transition from an $\sim(L/M)^{0.7}$ amplitude scaling to a steeper $\sim(L/M)^{1.5}$ scaling, occurring near the G/K-dwarf boundary toward decreasing $L/M$. In contrast, 3D simulations predict an $\sim(L/M)^{0.9}$ scaling for K dwarfs, revealing tension between observations and first-principles convection models. EPRV asteroseismology extends into the mid-K regime and exposes a steep mode-amplitude scaling that our 3D convection simulations do not reproduce. This discrepancy points to missing physics in our implementation of convection-pulsation coupling and/or limitations in the adopted modeling assumptions, motivating further theoretical investigation.

title: Quantitative Volume Estimate on Singular Sets of One-phase Free Boundary Problems in Ricci Limit Spaces
abstract: We study limit solutions of the one-phase free boundary problem on noncollapsed Ricci limit spaces. We introduce a quantitative stratification $\mathcal{S}^k_{\varepsilon,r}$ of the singular set of the free boundary that simultaneously captures the approximate splitting of the ambient space and the approximate homogeneity and translational invariance of the solution. We also introduce a new truncated parabolic Weiss quantity that provides quantitative homogeneity via pinching across scales. Although this quantity may not be uniformly bounded across all small scales, it effectively shows that, among the first $j$ scales in a fixed decreasing geometric progression, at most $C\sqrt{j}$ scales fail to exhibit quantitative homogeneity. Such slow growth in $j$ enables us to adapt the covering argument of Cheeger and Naber [arXiv:1103.1819] to show, for every $η>0$, a $Cr^{n-k-η}$ upper bound for the volume of the $r$-tubular neighborhood of the $k$-th quantitative singular stratum, $\mathcal{S}^k_{\varepsilon,r}$. The same tubular-neighborhood estimate holds for the effective stratum $\mathcal S_\varepsilon^k$, and in particular we get the Minkowski dimension bound $\dim_{\mathcal M} \mathcal S_\varepsilon^k \le k$, from which the previously known sharp bound $\dim_{\mathcal H} \mathrm{Sing} \le n-3$ in Chan, Zhang, and Zhu [arXiv:2112.06962] follows. As another corollary, we prove that the free boundary admits a Hölder manifold structure away from a set of Minkowski dimension at most $n-3$.

title: Practical wavelength selection for quantum-augmented networks over shared optical fiber
abstract: In a quantum augmented network, sharing optical fiber with classical traffic requires quantum wavelength selection to balance logical fidelity, block acceptance, and classical data reception. Here we develop a wavelength-selection framework for an error-corrected three-stage quantum communication protocol. Under a thermal-background model with independent errors, an ideal one-photon receiver, and ideal recovery, we derive an accepted qubit channel and a key-independent lower bound on logical entanglement fidelity. Combining this bound with block acceptance gives an entanglement-fidelity yield bound, which we maximize over evaluated wavelengths subject to fidelity and classical link-budget requirements. For the Steane [[7,1,3]] code at 5 km per traversal and -10 dBm per classical channel, the largest fidelity certificate occurs near 1537 nm, whereas the largest yield bound occurs near 1551 nm. Along the 1.25 Gb/s classical link budget with 0.2% base error, the optimized yield bound falls below 10^-6 near 10 km per traversal, while fidelity remains certified at 0.99 or higher at longer spans. These results distinguish fidelity and yield constraints and identify certified operating regions for quantum-augmented networks sharing optical fiber.

title: Classification of quantum states through conserved operators
abstract: Determining whether quantum states can be interconverted by a prescribed set of transformations is a fundamental problem in quantum information. Here we develop a general classification framework based on conserved operators (COs), i.e., not necessarily hermitian matrices having the state of interest as an eigenstate. We first show that COs belonging to the algebra generating the allowed transformations can be obtained from the kernel of a quantum covariance matrix. Their number determines the dimension of the accessible orbit, while their algebraic structure and eigenvalues provide further constraints on state convertibility. We establish general bounds on the number of COs and prove that highest-weight states, like separable states in the case of $n$ qudits, attain the maximum. We also show how these operators generate parent Hamiltonians having the characterized state as an exact ground state. We then also consider positive zero-eigenvalue COs, which encode forbidden directions of reduced density matrices and incorporate rank-based constraints into the same framework. Applying this approach to multiqubit SLOCC, we obtain complementary classifications from algebraic and rank COs. While for $n\leq 3$ qubits both lead to the usual classes, for $n=4$ qubits they distinguish 17 and 20 types separately, and 29 when combined. The combined classification yields 287 fixed types and $4$ continuous families for $n=5$ qubits, and 4926 fixed types and 147 continuous families for $n=6$ qubits, providing, to our knowledge, the most refined exhaustive classification of SLOCC-convertibility classes based on such data.

title: Do As I Do, Not As I Say: On-Policy Distillation Inherits the Teacher in Vision-Language Models
abstract: Improving the reasoning capabilities of vision-language models (VLMs) often relies on post-training with supervision from stronger models. Two common strategies are supervised fine-tuning (SFT), which trains on teacher-generated demonstrations, and on-policy distillation (OPD), which provides teacher feedback on trajectories generated by the student itself. While OPD can be more data-efficient by supervising student-generated trajectories, it is unclear how the teacher's supervision at each state affects the student's learned behavior. To study this question, we conduct a controlled comparison of OPD and filtered SFT across data budgets and tasks where the teacher exhibits different levels of reliability, and analyze how these differences shape student accuracy and completion behavior. Across the two tasks, we find that OPD is effective only when the teacher remains reliable on student-generated trajectories. On ChartQA, where the teacher completes 99% of its solutions, OPD trained on only 10% of the data comes within 1.4 accuracy points of full-data SFT. In contrast, on Geometry3K, where the teacher fails to complete 22% of its solutions, OPD underperforms SFT by 7.9 points, with most of the gap explained by incomplete responses. More strikingly, starting OPD from an SFT student reduces its completion rate from 76% to 62%, effectively erasing the completion behavior learned through SFT. Filtering teacher demonstrations for completeness alone recovers much of SFT's advantage. These results show that on-policy supervision can transfer not only teacher knowledge but also persistent failure modes on student-visited states. Code is available at https://github.com/ffy208/opd-inherits-teacher-vlm.

title: DeSpatial: The devil of Agentic Spatial Reasoning Lies in 3D Itself
abstract: Spatial agents have access to reconstruction and segmentation tools, yet inconsistent predictions and fragmented object identities can prevent their outputs from becoming reliable 3D scene information. A simple oracle experiment exposes this perception bottleneck: replacing tool-predicted perception with ground-truth 3D bounding boxes raises an agent to nearly full score across five object-centric VSI-Bench tasks, while retaining the same reasoning tools. Motivated by this finding, we believe the devil of spatial reasoning lies in 3D itself, and introduce DeSpatial(Devil of Spatial), which explicitly decomposes spatial understanding into perception and reasoning. DeSpatial has a shared 3D perception tool to reconcile independent perception outputs into a unified, metric, gravity-aligned 3D scene. This perception tool has two core components: a) a joint segmentation--depth co-refinement module that consolidates masks of the same object and removes projection artifacts caused by inconsistent segmentation and depth within a single frame; b) a cross-view instance fusion module that consolidate voxel-overlapping instances but not allowed to merge same-frame instances. This fusion module additionally fuses spatially disjoint fragments caused by insufficient multi-view observations, by checking their 3D structure and source mask appearance. After receiving the complete and unified 3D scene information, the agent chooses reasoning or computational tools to solve the spatial problem. DeSpatial achieves leading performance on VSI-Bench, MindCube-Tiny, and ViewSpatial, with additional long-video results on VSI-SUPER, revealing the bottleneck of spatial understanding lies in a precise 3D perception itself.

title: Normal complex surface singularities with rational homology disk smoothings
abstract: We prove that a normal surface singularity whose minimal good resolution graph has at least two nodes does not admit a rational homology disk smoothing. Together with the earlier graph classifications and the analytic classifications of Fowler and Wahl, this gives a complete classification of normal surface singularities admitting rational homology disk smoothings and proves Wahl's conjecture. The same argument also proves Wahl's Rational Conjecture.

title: Quadratic fields of values of finite solvable groups
abstract: We show that if $G$ is a finite solvable group such that $E = \mathbb Q(\{χ(g)\, |\, χ\in{\rm Irr}(G),\ g \in G\})$ is an extension of degree 2 over the rationals, then $E = \mathbb Q(\sqrt{\pm d})$ for a positive integer $d$ all of whose prime divisors lie in $\{2, 3, 5\}$. Moreover, if $G$ has a composition factor of order 7, then either $E = \mathbb Q(\sqrt{2})$ or $E = \mathbb Q(\sqrt{-3})$. This provides a partial answer to a question of G. Navarro.

title: One Bias Score, Two Factors: How Mitigations Affect Option Bias in Multiple-Choice Evaluation
abstract: Reordering multiple-choice options can change a model's answer, an effect studied as selection bias (a preference for certain option letters) and as order sensitivity (changes in answers across option orderings). We connect these perspectives through the pooled selection-rate standard deviation (pooled SD), which measures how unevenly option letters are selected across questions and orderings. When every option of each question appears equally often at each position, the pooled SD is exactly the product of two label-free factors: the flip rate and the positional skew. The flip rate is the fraction of questions whose chosen option changes across orderings; the positional skew is the standard deviation of option-letter selection rates among those questions. Across 41 checkpoints and 12 benchmarks, the flip rate tracks accuracy and output uncertainty, while the positional skew tracks the estimated option-symbol prior. Prior correction for selection bias mainly reduces the positional skew. Aggregating each ordering with its reversal, a mitigation for order sensitivity, mainly reduces the flip rate. Both reduce the range of accuracy across correct-answer letters by similar amounts, but aggregation leaves fewer model-rank reversals. Applying prior correction before aggregation reduces both factors and further narrows this accuracy range. However, aggregation lowers the flip rate partly by settling questions on the same wrong option. We therefore recommend reporting both factors to distinguish mitigation effects, alongside accuracy to distinguish stability from correctness.

title: Automorphisms of twisted Chevalley groups of type ${}^2E_6$ over local rings
abstract: We classify abstract automorphisms of the elementary and full twisted Chevalley groups of type ${}^2E_6$ over commutative local rings with involution and $2$ invertible, for both isogeny types. Every automorphism is standard, with no invertibility assumption on $3$. In the adjoint case, it has a unique expression as a composition of conjugation by an element of the full twisted group and a ring automorphism commuting with the involution. For the simply connected form, the full group equals its elementary subgroup, and the factors are strictly inner, diagonal, and ring automorphisms. The main step replaces a linear change of basis by a group element. Invariant alternating tensors determine the transported Chevalley bracket. We correct this bracket over a faithfully flat local extension and descend the resulting conjugating element by uniqueness. Root-subgroup relations then recover the coefficient automorphism.

title: The Komlós Problem in Matrix-Multiplication Time
abstract: We give a randomized algorithm that, for an $m\times n$ matrix whose columns have Euclidean norm at most one, finds a signing with discrepancy below $99$ in expected $\widetilde O(L_{\mathrm{in}}+n^ω)$ bit operations, where $L_{\mathrm{in}}$ is the input encoding length and $ω$ is the exponent of matrix multiplication. The previous fastest algorithm with a constant discrepancy bound, due to Li, is deterministic and uses $O(mn+n^{ω+2}\log^3 n)$ arithmetic operations. We build on the spectral signing framework of Guo, Fang, and Lu and of Li, which rounds a single fractional coloring while one spectral potential controls every row. Li's potential tracks a top eigenvalue, and the gap below that eigenvalue, which can be of order $1/n$, limits the length of every step. We replace it with a resolvent potential that is smooth without any gap condition, and we draw step signs at random, so that the potential only needs to be concave while progress is measured separately. Our key insight is to reuse a single subspace of directions throughout a batch of steps, thereby using only one spectral computation, so that the more expensive linear algebraic operations are paid for only polylogarithmically often at each scale. Within a batch, we sample directions from a Gaussian completion matrix whose inverse we maintain under rank-one row replacements. Finally, we use a finite-precision analysis to prove stability of the algorithm and attain the bit-complexity bound.

title: Quantum-Corrected and Hairy Black Holes via Analogue Gravity
abstract: This thesis maps two exotic black-hole geometries onto the transonic flow of a de Laval nozzle and reads their perturbative response in aerodynamic variables. The first is the hairy black hole of gravitational decoupling, constrained by the dominant energy condition and by the existence of a horizon. The second is the Calmet-Kuipers metric, short-ranged and governed by the single Wilson coefficient of the dimension-six operator that the two-loop Goroff-Sagnotti divergence identifies. Perturbations of spin 0, 1/2, 1 and 2 reduce to a Schrödinger-type wave equation, whose spectrum the Mashhoon method returns as a whole overtone tower in closed form, every frequency damped. The two corrections are distinguished by which channel responds and by how strongly all of them do, the quantum coupling moving the quality factor by up to 37% in the scalar and Dirac channels and by about 10% in the other two, while the hair acts on every channel alike. Identifying the two tortoise coordinates turns the equality of the potentials into a Sturm-Liouville problem, so that the prescribed barrier fixes the wall profile and with it the flow variables and the thrust coefficient. The hair is felt across the whole divergent section, whereas the quantum correction registers only near the throat and grows as the inverse fourth power of the mass, which confines it to primordial black holes. The analogy is kinematical, so the duct reproduces the scattering of perturbations off these geometries without reproducing the field equations behind them.

title: Halve-Then-Greedy: Adaptive Sampling for Posterior Success with Near-Optimal Instance Dependence
abstract: We study fixed-budget adaptive experimentation aimed at maximizing the probability of obtaining sufficient posterior evidence that a recommended design's mean performance exceeds a target. Unlike best-arm identification, this objective does not require finding the best design. For Gaussian bandits with a Gaussian prior, we propose \emph{Halve-Then-Greedy} (HTG), which combines a large initial balanced allocation, successive halving, and posterior-greedy sampling. We prove instance-dependent, finite-budget exponential bounds on posterior-failure probability that capture both separation from unfavorable arms and the presence of multiple favorable arms. On one-positive-arm families, we establish an asymptotic sample-complexity lower bound that HTG matches up to a logarithmic factor. We further analyze uniform sampling and sequential halving, revealing regimes where they require more samples than HTG by linear and logarithmic factors, respectively. Simulations illustrate HTG's sample-efficiency advantages and their dependence on instance structure.

title: MoCaP: Mobile Code-as-Policies for Zero-Shot Mobile Manipulation from Passive Human Videos
abstract: Passive human videos of everyday activity offer robots access to a massive amount of human experience without requiring a demonstration for each task. However, using this experience requires recovering knowledge from unstructured video recordings and adapting it to a different body (i.e., the robot). To overcome these challenges, we present mobile code-as-policy (MoCaP), an agentic framework that turns passive human video recordings into guidance for an end-to-end mobile manipulation policy. MoCaP extracts spatial memory and cues of how people prepare to interact with objects, which inform navigation and the search for a manipulation-ready configuration. Guided by passive human experience and current observations, MoCaP uses a closed-loop code-as-policy to coordinate planning and tool use primitives to solve motions under the robot's geometry and kinematic constraints. On a real mobile manipulator, MoCaP achieves 80% success on each of two mobile manipulation tasks in an indoor environment whereas existing approaches cannot succeed at the task. Video-derived spatial memory improves object-navigation success from 70% to 100%, and human approach prior raises the rate of finding a reachable base pose from 0% to 100% at an unfavorable start location. Videos and code are available on the project website: https://mocap-7.github.io/MoCAP-page/.

title: EigDiff: Eigensample Diffusion - or how to significantly reduce training dataset size with marginal performance variation?
abstract: Diffusion models are notoriously expensive to train, requiring large-scale datasets to learn how to gradually reverse the noise from images over multiple small denoising steps. Current approaches focus on distilling the number of diffusion steps, neglecting potential redundancies of the training data. In this paper, we explore the potential of harnessing eigensamples to train diffusion models on significantly smaller datasets, while preserving model performance. To mitigate the sensitivity to affine transformations of eigenimages, we harness the latent space of a pre-trained CLIP model. We next compute latent eigenvectors by performing principal component analysis (PCA) in CLIP space. Further, we employ eigenvectors as reference points to guide the selection of a representative training set comprising comprising both exemplars (images whose embeddings are closest to eigenvectors) and diverse images. Our comprehensive experiments with different diffusion models applied on multiple datasets indicate that our approach (EigDiff) can reduce training data by up to 14x and accelerate subset selection by up to 1607x, with marginal performance differences.

title: monoprop: Scaling Pauli and Majorana propagation via Anticommutation Indices
abstract: We introduce monoprop, an open-source, massively parallel operator-propagation framework for fermion and qubit bases. For $N$ qubits or modes, existing codes represent each of the $K$ tracked operator terms (Pauli strings or products of Majorana operators) as a $2N$-bit string, testing each for anticommutation with the gate at $O(KN)$ cost per gate. Here, we introduce the anticommutation index which rapidly looks up the terms anticommuting with a gate. A local gate changes only the terms that touch its sites, and when terms are truncated to act on few sites, only a fraction $\sim1/N$ touch any given qubit or mode, and we use this to prove the time per gate scales as $O(K/N)$. This counterintuitive result tells us that for a fixed number of terms, increasing the number of sites can make things faster. We demonstrate this numerically, and show monoprop scales almost ideally to 8192 cores, tracking $9.5\times10^{10}$ terms. Beyond propagation, we present memory-efficient surrogate graphs, which record one propagation and replay it at new angles, for fast energy re-estimation and parameter gradients, and an efficient method for finding energy-minimising gates and optimal angles for simulating adaptive quantum-chemistry circuits.

title: Imperfect Is Perfect: Learned Column Prefilling for Branch-Price-and-Cut
abstract: Column generation folklore warns that initial columns hurt: a warm start may bias the dual and slow the root of branch-price-and-cut. We show the opposite once the columns are imperfect in the right way. Preloading the support of the optimal root LP, the best columns one could know in advance, fails to finish on half of our hardest instances; a pool of ordinary routes that need not belong to any optimal solution, held outside the master and priced at the current smoothed dual, speeds the root up. Because the columns need not be optimal, producing them becomes a learning task: a neural edge scorer guides a constructive generator that builds the pool in seconds. A second network predicts the initial center of Wentges smoothing from the instance file, and with it the direction of the smoothed pricing queries; the solver's own updates run unchanged. With prefill and center in place, exact pricing dominates root pricing time, so we rebuild bucket-graph labeling around its dominance test for the GPU and certify on the CPU. Inside RouteOpt, the state-of-the-art exact solver for capacitated vehicle routing, the pipeline reaches the same certified root bound in 13.2% of vanilla RouteOpt's root pricing time over 95 instances with 300 to 1000 customers, prefill alone in 26.1%, and 17.5 times faster in the best case. In an exact branch-price-and-cut solver for unrelated parallel machine scheduling, prefill with smoothing and the learned center certifies all 25 benchmark instances, 12 times faster than the solver's own column generation, which certifies 20 of them.

title: A Physical-Space Approach to Modified Scattering for the 3D Hartree Equation: Full-Space and Robin Half-Space
abstract: We prove global well-posedness and modified scattering for the three-dimensional Hartree equation for small data in $H^{0,k}$, with $k>\frac12$ on $\mathbb R^3$ and $k=1$ on the half-space $\mathbb R^3_+$ with a real Robin boundary condition. For these data, the nonlinear and asymptotic analysis is carried out entirely in physical space, combining slow-growth estimates for Galilean vector fields with a scale-invariant interaction estimate. For the half-space problem, we construct an extension intertwining the Robin and free flows and a boundary-adapted field that overcome the loss of normal Galilean symmetry.

title: Reducing QUBO Complexity in Drone Delivery Through Classical Feasibility Preprocessing
abstract: Drone-delivery planning combines routing decisions with operational constraints such as payload capacity and limited onboard energy, resulting in combinatorial optimization problems that can become costly to encode directly in binary form. This work investigates a hybrid quantum--classical approach in which candidate drone missions are generated and evaluated classically before constructing a quadratic unconstrained binary optimization (QUBO) model for mission selection. Payload- and energy-infeasible missions are removed during preprocessing, while the reduced QUBO is solved using exact enumeration, simulated annealing (SA), and the Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm (QAOA), with mixed-integer linear programming (MILP) used as a classical reference. Experiments on controlled synthetic delivery instances evaluate solution quality, the effect of preprocessing, and computational scaling. Exact QUBO optimization reproduces the MILP optimum on the evaluated small instances, while SA achieves $100\%$ feasibility with a median optimality gap of $0\%$. Combined payload-and-energy preprocessing reduces the mean number of QUBO variables by $29.60\%$ and quadratic interactions by $49.20\%$, while reducing mean SA runtime by $31.26\%$. In contrast, the evaluated shallow statevector-based QAOA configuration achieves lower feasibility and is restricted to small QUBO instances. These results indicate that, in the considered setting, the main practical benefit of the hybrid architecture comes from classical feasibility preprocessing that reduces the binary search space before QUBO-based optimization.

title: Skew fields of non-commutative meromorphic functions affiliated to finite operator algebras
abstract: We embed skew fields of meromorphic functions in several non-commuting variables into the topological $*-$algebra of closed linear operators affiliated to a finite von Neumann algebra, $\mathfrak{M}$, with faithful, normal tracial state, $τ$. Namely, let $\mathscr{O} _d (r)$, $r \in (0, +\infty]$, denote the rings of formal power series in $d \in \mathbb{N}$ non-commuting variables with ``radius of convergence" at least $r$ and let $Ξ\in \mathfrak{M} ^{1\times d}$ be a tuple of row-norm $<r$ with the property that there exist no non-zero trace-class operators $T_1, \cdots, T_d \in \mathscr{B} (L^2 (\mathfrak{M}, τ))$ obeying $\sum _j [T_j , Ξ_j] =0$. Then the unital homomorphism $\mathscr{O} _d (r) \rightarrow \mathfrak{M}$ defined by the evaluation, $\mathfrak{z} _j \mapsto Ξ_j$, extends to an embedding of the universal skew field of fractions of $\mathscr{O} _d (r)$ into the $*-$algebra of closed operators affiliated to $\mathfrak{M}$. In their $L^2-$homology theory of von Neumann algebras, Connes and Shlyakhtenko defined a certain quantity, $0 \leq Δ(Ξ) \leq d$, as the Murray--von Neumann co-dimension of the Hilbert module generated by all $d-$tuples of finite rank operators obeying the above commutator condition with $Ξ\in \mathfrak{M} ^{1\times d}$. As demonstrated by Mai, Speicher and Yin, this $Δ$ measures, in a certain precise sense, the algebraic independence of the components of $Ξ$. Connes--Shlyakhtenko proved that $Δ$ is an upper bound for Voiculescu's non-microstates free entropy dimension, $δ^* (Ξ)$, and remark that it is of interest to determine whether these two quantities are equal. Using non-commutative function theory, we show that this is generally not the case, by constructing a triple of self-adjoint operators, $Ξ= (Ξ_1,Ξ_2,Ξ_3)$, for which this inequality is strict, $δ^*(Ξ) < Δ(Ξ)$.

title: Zhang twists for semigroups and groupoids, with applications to Steinberg algebras
abstract: Zhang twists provide a powerful mechanism for deforming graded algebras, while preserving their graded module categories. We extend this theory by introducing Zhang twists for graded semigroups and graded ample groupoids. We show that the twisting construction preserves a broad class of semigroup structures, and that two graded monoids are twists of each other if and only if their categories of graded sets are pointedly equivalent. We show that Zhang twists are compatible with noncommutative Stone duality: twists on graded-Boolean inverse semigroups are in correspondence with those on the associated graded ample groupoids. Moreover, in the setting of Steinberg algebras we prove that twisting the groupoid gives the same result as twisting the corresponding algebra. These results provide a unified framework linking graded semigroups, inverse semigroup duality, ample groupoids, and graded algebras, while extending the scope of Zhang twists to settings arising from symbolic dynamics, graph algebras, and Steinberg algebras.

title: Can LLMs Anticipate Their Cruxes?
abstract: To use language models to help us make decisions we would like to understand the rationale behind the language model's outputs. In principle, the language model provides its rationale as part of its text output. However, the sheer volume of text makes this hard to use in practice. In this paper, we are interested in extracting the cruxes that lead a model to recommend one action over another. We take a crux to be a sub-question that a model's rollouts disagree on, where changing its value may have altered the conclusion. A crux is therefore a property of the distribution of a model's rollouts, not of any one rollout. We consider three strategies of increasing computational cost. First, we just ask a model to identify, a priori, what the cruxes of a decision will be. Second, we have the model actually go through the process of generating a response and then extract the cruxes that arose in its reasoning. Finally, we generate many responses and extract the cruxes by comparing the reasoning across the rollouts. We make this last procedure computationally tractable with cheap calls to a reranker, an estimated 86 times less compute than a judge. We then conduct an extensive empirical evaluation to assess whether the computationally inexpensive options are sufficient. They are not. Across domains and models, we find that a model's a priori assessment of the cruxes has little relation to the factors that are actually identified as important a posteriori. Using a single rollout helps, but is still inadequate for identifying the full set of cruxes. Accordingly, for high-stakes decisions (and to understand the space of language model decision making) the many rollout procedure is unavoidable.

title: Mind the Tail: Data Selection Through Sparse Concepts
abstract: Data selection reallocates training support across visual concepts, including objects, attributes, color, texture, and backgrounds. Different allocation strategies may produce varied downstream model behavior, especially for tail concepts supported by only a few samples. Discarding them can hurt test-time robustness, while overemphasizing samples lying on category boundaries may introduce unstable training signals. This work explicitly investigates this relationship across fine-grained, spurious-correlation, and general image classification, as well as multimodal pretraining. Specifically, we use sparse autoencoders (SAEs) to extract concept activations from individual images. During selection, we accumulate the dataset-level concept support for each added sample. Applying diminishing returns to this distribution down-weights well-represented concepts and shifts the focus to the distribution tail. We then incorporate local support to find samples that reliably strengthen under-supported concepts. Empirical results show consistent improvements over strong data selection baselines across all benchmarks. We also reveal the connection between concepts our method enhances and the induced behavioral changes, including improved robustness against out-of-distribution and spurious contexts. This work establishes concept support, beyond individual sample importance, as a useful principle for data-efficient and robust learning.

title: Deep Reinforcement Learning for HPC Job Scheduling: A Statistical Evaluation
abstract: Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL) offers learned job selection for High-Performance Computing (HPC), but performance against heuristics alone does not establish value beyond action masking. Six DRL treatments are compared: Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO), Advantage Actor-Critic (A2C), and Deep Q-Network (DQN), each with and without masking. Three heuristics and a seed-paired masked uniform random control provide baselines across ten seeds on two real Slurm (Simple Linux Utility for Resource Management) workload traces, one homogeneous and one heterogeneous, under a common non-parametric framework. All masked treatments complete evaluation, whereas unmasked treatments are truncated. On the homogeneous trace, no masked DRL treatment significantly improves average waiting time or average and maximum bounded slowdown over the control. On the heterogeneous trace, MaskablePPO improves all three metrics relative to the control. Its average waiting time is equivalent to that of the three heuristics within a 10% margin, and its maximum bounded slowdown is 22% lower than that of Last-Come, First-Served (LCFS). MaskablePPO has the leading average waiting-time rank among complete treatments on both traces, but Nemenyi comparisons detect no significant difference from MaskableA2C. Among masked variants, MaskablePPO has the lowest recorded mean training time, while MaskableDQN has the lowest mean decision latency. These findings distinguish completion from baseline-specific scheduling gains and support including a masked random control when assessing the value of learned selection.

title: Length control for foliations by Jordan curves via smooth quasiconformal maps
abstract: Let $Ω\subsetneq\mathbb C$ be a non-empty simply connected domain and $0<p<2$. Bouchala and Koskela [Proc. Amer. Math. Soc. (2024)] proved that there exists a quasiconformal map $f:\mathbb D\toΩ$ such that $\int_0^1\ell(f(r S^1))^p\,dr<\infty$, and asked whether this conclusion holds at $p=2$, or even for every $0<p<2+\varepsilon$ with some $\varepsilon>0$. We answer this question affirmatively with $\varepsilon=2/157$ by constructing a single smooth $5$-quasiconformal map $f:\mathbb D\toΩ$ satisfying this integrability condition simultaneously for every $0<p<2+2/157$.

title: Operator Algebraic Quantum Hypergroups
abstract: We develop a theory of operator algebraic quantum hypergroups and their representations, formulated using a special case of the algebraic quantum hypergroup framework of van Daele and Delvaux. As part of the axioms, every operator algebraic quantum hypergroup admits a dual object of the same type. We prove that a certain universal completion in the compact case satisfies the axioms of an earlier notion of a compact quantum hypergroup in the sense of the second author and Chapovsky. As part of this theory, we discuss their (co)amenability properties. We consider examples induced by conditional expectations of algebraic quantum groups satisfying certain properties, which include quantum hypergroups corresponding to double cosets and automorphisms of quantum groups, and quantum hypergroups induced by representation categories of Kac type compact quantum groups.

title: Audio-Visual Dog Identification and Tracking in Real-World Videos
abstract: Identifying individual dogs from barks in real-world videos remains challenging and largely unexplored. Solving this problem would enable long-term behavioral analysis, veterinary monitoring, and animal welfare monitoring by attributing vocalizations and behaviors to the correct individual. Real-world videos are challenging because multiple dogs may bark simultaneously, become occluded, or move in and out of view. Prior studies show that canine vocalizations and visual appearance contain discriminative identity information, but these modalities have largely been studied independently. We present a multimodal dog-fingerprinting framework combining visual identification, multiple-object tracking, and canine vocal fingerprinting to associate bark events with individual dogs while maintaining persistent profiles. The framework synchronizes bark events with tracked dogs and updates profiles using visual appearance and vocal characteristics, enabling identification despite occlusion, overlapping vocalizations, and off-screen barking. We also introduce a benchmark of 46 real-world videos containing 213 manually annotated bark events. Our framework correctly localizes the active visible dog in 61.83% of visible events at IoU $\geq 0.30$ and achieves a 91.33% F1 score for visible versus off-screen barking detection.

title: Variable Masking for Climate Emulation in ACE
abstract: In the recent AI Model Intercomparison Project (AIMIP) benchmark, the ACE2.1-ERA5 emulator was shown to underestimate the true near-surface warming trend both during the training period and the out-of-sample extrapolation period. In this work, we present M-ACE2S (Masked-ACE2S), a modified version of the stochastic ACE2S model, which uses variable masking during training and reduces the reliance of M-ACE2S on any single input channel. We show that M-ACE2S improves long-term near-surface air temperature prediction. We also present a novel data normalization strategy called "global mean removal", which, combined with masking, further improves the near-surface temperature forecasts. We show that M-ACE2S outperforms the ACE2S baseline on in-sample data for ERA5 while improving training stability and generalizability of near-surface temperature to unseen forcing when paired with global mean removal.

title: LWM-TF: A Wireless Foundation Model on 5G NR Time-Frequency Resource Grids
abstract: Received OFDM grids preserve both pilot and payload observations, yet wireless foundation models are rarely pre-trained on them. We introduce LWM-TF, a 9.58M-parameter factorized masked autoencoder pre-trained on complex 5G NR uplink grids taken after the FFT and before channel estimation. Each block attends first across OFDM symbols and then across resource blocks and receive antennas, and the mask follows the same two axes. Because the payload phase is unpredictable, the model reconstructs the normalized log-power of each masked token and predicts its scale separately; ablations show that the two terms are complementary and that this target outperforms complex-signal reconstruction. The encoder is pre-trained on 850,496 physical uplink shared channel (PUSCH) slots from a 10^6-slot dataset simulated with the NR transmit chain under various channel conditions. With the encoder frozen, linear probes classify modulation, predict CRC success, and detect UE mobility. On a separately generated test set, 16 labeled slots per class give 0.85 modulation accuracy, 0.82 CRC area under the ROC curve (AUROC), and 0.73 mobility AUROC, ahead of a supervised CNN on every paired draw. With 10,000 labels the probes reach 0.94, 0.96, and 0.92, well above engineered receiver statistics, and detect mobility where the CNN stays at chance. Without any impairment labels, distances in the frozen feature space flag unseen waveform impairments with 0.78 macro AUROC, against 0.68 for receiver statistics. A single pre-trained encoder thus provides receiver features that transfer across tasks, most strongly when labels are scarce.

title: Measure Theory in Convergence Spaces Part II: Abstract Integration in Net Convergence Structures
abstract: The construction of a coherent and general integration procedure is the central question of this second part of our study of measure theory in convergence spaces. We define, and establish convergence theorems for such process of integration, called the net Riemann integration, in convergence groups and commutative monoids, preserving the prescribed convergence throughout. The underlying interchange theorem admits noncommutative groups and requires right completeness only at the cardinality of the error family. Under intrinsic stability assumptions, countable error control therefore needs only sequential completeness, even for arbitrary integration nets, from which we also stablish a general version of Henstock's lemma. The resulting uniform theorems reaches incomplete ranges in which no complete subspace contains a tail of the approximating integrals. In the ordered locally solid convergence theory side, countability of the inner direction replaces countable accessibility of the approximants, and local existence arguments yield monotone and dominated convergence and, under additional controller assumptions, a further extension through increasing integrable barriers with pointwise coverage and uniformly vanishing excess primitives. This constructs the limiting integral without a common integrable envelope and gives uniform control of primitive variation. We finish with two appendices on new and general results of abstract metrization of net convergences and related topics.

title: MASON: Materials Atomistic Structure builder Operated in Natural language
abstract: Building reliable atomistic models is a critical and often challenging step in first-principles calculations. Although large language model agents can assist with structure generation, they lack direct capabilities for crystallographic operations and therefore struggle to construct complex structures reliably. Here we present MASON, an AI-native toolkit for atomistic structure construction that can be invoked by agents through the Model Context Protocol (MCP). In an end-to-end example, an agent builds a CO/Pt(111) adsorption model from a natural language request. By equipping agents with dedicated structure-building tools, MASON enables reliable and efficient atomistic model construction and provides a foundation for autonomous first-principles workflows.

title: CausalEvo: Causal Skill Self-Evolution for Health LLM Agents
abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents for health can accumulate reusable textual skills from task feedback, such as calculation criteria, measurement time points, and formula units. Deciding which skills to retain is consequential: useful rules improve later answers, while faulty generalizations propagate errors. We propose CausalEvo, a method for causal skill self-evolution that estimates the relative effects of deliberately changed skill sets while holding the model weights, feedback cases, and rule count fixed. At each evolution step, a frozen LLM proposes candidate rules, which are pooled with the incumbent skills so that the current skill set remains a feasible choice. Paired skill replacements against shared background rules are scored on the same feedback cases; least squares converts the score differences into relative skill values, and the top-ranked rules are retained, favoring incumbents on ties. A decision-loss bound separates candidate support, approximation, and estimation errors. On six MedCalc-Bench-Verified tasks with 120 held-out cases, CausalEvo achieves 60.00% accuracy, compared with 55.83% for SkillOpt and 51.67% without skills. Across the recorded training configurations, which use different optimization budgets, it consumes 55.6% fewer training tokens than SkillOpt. Gains concentrate in particular calculations alongside regressions on others, and paired accuracy intervals include zero. CausalEvo turns task feedback into controlled decisions about skill retention and replacement. Project repository: https://github.com/txbrook/CausalEvo

title: Crossing numbers of simplicial complexes
abstract: This paper studies crossing numbers of $d$-dimensional simplicial complexes drawn in $\mathbb R^{2d}$ or $\mathbb S^{2d}$. We clarify and generalize a number of known results and conjectures from the graph case to higher dimensions: the crossing lemma (including the exceptional case of two-dimensional complexes drawn in dimension $4$), a generalized Harary-Hill conjecture (and evidence for it), existence of a midrange crossing constant (in a weak sense), and upper bound constructions based on stochastic geometry (related to Sylvester's problem) and the cyclic polytope. Some of our results are new even in the case of graphs: we give a simple proof of the Harary-Hill conjecture for antipodal drawings, and sharpen the threshold above which the rectilinear and spherical crossing numbers of the Erdős-Rényi random graph behave like those of the complete graph.

title: Failure Is the Mother of Success: Recovering Supervision with Grounding Hindsight
abstract: When every rollout for a problem fails, GRPO receives neither a successful exemplar nor a nonzero group-relative advantage, so it learns nothing from exactly the problems it most needs to learn. The failed reasoning can nevertheless suggest what to try next. We present Replay-Selected Hindsight Distillation (RSHD), which turns failed attempts into an additional, tested source of supervision during GRPO training. The policy writes a corrective note about each failed attempt without seeing a reference answer or solution, then re-solves the problem with the note in context. A note is admitted only if its replays succeed more often than the original group did, after screening for notes that state the answer, and an admitted replay is distilled into the plain-prompt policy. Because admission is decided by fresh successes rather than by the failed rollout itself, the procedure can recover supervision from groups in which every attempt failed, and it applies equally to failures in mixed groups. Only the policy is trained, the only judge is the outcome verifier, and deployment requires no notes or extra inference. Across model families and sizes and two training domains, RSHD consistently improves over GRPO on in-domain benchmarks, and the gains carry over to out-of-domain evaluation sets.

title: Testing Tail-Index Homogeneity via Exceedance-Covariate Independence
abstract: We propose a test of whether the tail index of a heavy-tailed outcome is homogeneous across observed covariates. The key observation is that, under tail-index homogeneity, normalized log exceedances are asymptotically independent of the covariates even when tail frequencies vary with them. This leads to a simple-to-implement permutation test based on distance covariance, without estimating conditional tail indices or specifying the form of tail-index heterogeneity. For the global and locally balanced versions, we establish validity for order-statistic thresholds and give conditions for consistency and local power. Local balancing selects extremes within two covariate groups and can improve power when tail selection concentrates the covariates. Simulations illustrate these gains. In French motor insurance data, upper conditional quantiles vary with risk characteristics, but the tail-index tests do not reject a common tail index.

title: Acceleration and its Limits in Gaussian Variational Inference
abstract: We study whether the classical momentum-based acceleration that improves the condition-number dependence of gradient descent from $κ$ to $\sqrtκ$ for strongly convex, smooth objectives extends to Gaussian variational inference (GVI) for strongly log-concave, log-smooth target distributions. With exact Gaussian expectations, a convex composite formulation of GVI yields the classical accelerated $\sqrtκ$ convergence rate. However, when only pointwise derivatives are available, we construct a family of strongly log-concave targets for which any randomized algorithm requires $κ^{1-o(1)}$ queries to achieve a fixed objective accuracy, even when the initial objective gap is bounded independently of $κ$. Thus curvature bounds alone cannot guarantee uniform accelerated total-query complexity. We then ask which additional structure permits acceleration and give positive examples: under a Hessian-Lipschitz assumption, variance-reduced stochastic methods yield accelerated guarantees when the Hessian variation is sufficiently small. Finally, experiments on real datasets show substantial empirical speedups from acceleration across a broad range of methods.

title: GeoMix: A Bayesian Framework for Stratigraphic and Geotechnical Inference
abstract: Accurate characterisation of subsea sediments is essential for engineering projects such as offshore wind farms, but the challenging environment and large spatial domains involved make dense geotechnical measurements impractical. Seismic traces offer a cheap, abundant complement, yet their geotechnical interpretation relies on subjective judgement, leading to biased, hard-to-validate predictions of sediment structure. To address this, we introduce GeoMix, a fully Bayesian hierarchical framework for jointly inferring geological stratigraphy and geotechnical properties from seismic and geotechnical data. GeoMix uses a Potts Markov random field to represent spatially coherent geology organised into distinct stratigraphic layers. Labels derived from seismic interpretation are linked to the latent stratigraphy through an observation model that captures elevated uncertainty near transitions between strata. Conditional on the latent stratigraphy, geotechnical properties are modelled using class-specific Gaussian processes, with scalable likelihood evaluation enabled by a grouped Vecchia approximation. Together, these components yield a unified latent-variable model capable of recovering stratigraphy, quantifying uncertainty, and predicting geotechnical properties across large three-dimensional domains. Simulation studies and an application to the IJmuiden Ver offshore wind farm show that GeoMix produces spatially coherent stratigraphic estimates and sediment predictions that are better calibrated and more accurate than existing approaches.

title: A Bayesian hierarchical push-forward method for cluster Randomized Controlled Trial power calculations in complex humanitarian settings
abstract: The design and evaluation of public health interventions in humanitarian crises demand rigorous yet flexible methodological approaches. Cluster-randomized controlled trials (cRCTs) are increasingly used to generate evidence in such settings, but trial conduct is frequently complicated by displacement, resource constraints, and cluster dropout. Although Bayesian methods provide a natural framework for hierarchical modeling, probabilistic uncertainty quantification, and the integration of prior knowledge, their use in cRCT design remains limited, particularly with respect to anticipating missingness. This paper introduces a Bayesian design strategy tailored for cRCTs in complex settings, motivated by a forthcoming trial in Cox's Bazar, Bangladesh, that will assess a community health worker adherence intervention for cardiovascular disease and hepatitis C. Our approach incorporates prior information on cluster and individual-level dropout into power and sample size calculations via a hierarchical model and push-forward distribution framework. Through simulation studies, we evaluate the performance of the proposed method under varying levels of missingness and correlation structures. The approach is then applied to inform the design of the Bangladesh trial. We disseminate our methods via a publicly-available R Shiny app to promote accessibility and usability to investigators. By formalizing Bayesian strategies that anticipate data loss, this work provides a foundation for more robust and efficient cRCTs in humanitarian contexts; therefore, strengthening the evidence base for health interventions in resource-limited and crisis-affected populations.

title: Beyond Match Results: Bayesian Mediation of Ability, Performance, and Winning in Professional Tennis
abstract: Match results measure competitive ability, but they do not explain how ability is expressed during play. Match statistics offer a natural mediator, however performance is usually measured over the same match as the outcome: a full-match statistic uses events that help determine the winner, while a first-set statistic is earlier but rests on fewer service points and still contributes to the result. Comparing the two therefore mixes timing and precision. We develop a Bayesian mediation framework for this problem. Dynamic abilities on hard, clay, and grass courts are estimated from previous seasons only and are linked to both players' service performance, and a Bradley--Terry model relates ability and performance to the match result. A control mediator samples the first set's number of service points from the full match, separating the measurement window from the point count. In 3,820 men's matches, the hard-court mediated share rises from 0.52 with a first-set mediator to 0.95 with a full-match mediator; the point-count contrast accounts for 0.30 of this gap and the window contrast for 0.13. The pattern replicates on the women's tour. Simulations and sensitivity analyzes examine the decomposition and assumptions needed for a causal interpretation.

title: Stationarity equations for fractional affine area measures: ellipsoid rigidity and polytopal solutions
abstract: Xi and Zhao established a first variation formula for affine inequalities involving radial mean bodies, and asked two geometric questions about the resulting stationarity equation: whether the bodies already known to satisfy it are the only ones, and whether its smooth solutions are exactly the ellipsoids. We answer both. Every strictly convex solution of the equation with $q>-1$, $q\ne0,n$ is an ellipsoid, which answers the second question affirmatively while replacing smoothness and everywhere positive Gauss curvature by strict convexity. Every full-dimensional facet-transitive polytope satisfies the equation, and so does the polar of every vertex-transitive polytope with respect to its volume centroid; the rhombic dodecahedron, the thirteen Catalan solids and the bipyramids over regular polygons other than the octahedron provide infinitely many affinely inequivalent solutions that are not affine images of regular polytopes or balls, so the answer to the first question is negative. The rigidity proof compares overlap integrals along a continuous Steiner path: stationarity forces an increase of order $o(t)$, whereas a nonaffine chord midpoint function forces an increase of order $t$. For negative parameters the required comparison rests on a minimization formula over bounded measurable auxiliary sets.

title: Learning to Read Out: Unembedding Dynamics in Language Model Pretraining
abstract: When does a language model acquire a capability? Developmental studies usually answer this by tracking when models start producing the correct token. But that prediction passes through the unembedding matrix, or readout, which is itself still being learned during pretraining. We show that a model's hidden states can encode task information before its own readout expresses it, so timelines read from outputs conflate what the model encodes with what its readout expresses. To track the readout directly, we introduce parameter-trajectory crosscoding, which fits one sparse dictionary to every token's readout row at every checkpoint. Unlike crosscoders on activations, it needs only checkpoint weights. We use it to locate a narrow early window, 0.4-1.1% of the way through Pythia's pretraining, in which the readout reorganizes and WordNet word categories become decodable from its rows. By then, linear probes on the hidden states already decode task information that the model's own outputs do not yet show. To test whether such gaps depend on how fast the readout learns, we pretrain small models from scratch that differ only in the readout's learning rate. We find that raising it makes the readout develop earlier and the gap close sooner, with little effect on final loss. Together, these results imply that early in training, where many developmental transitions are dated, a behavioral date can reflect when the readout learns to express task information and not when the model learns it.

title: On the Last-Iterate Convergence of Clipped Gradient Methods
abstract: In stochastic (strongly) convex optimization, establishing last-iterate convergence guarantees for first-order methods has recently garnered increasing attention, as this not only deepens the theoretical understanding of these algorithms but also aligns more closely with practice. Notably, people have demonstrated that one of the most famous, simple, and popular methods, Stochastic Gradient Descent ($\mathtt{SGD}$), provably achieves last-iterate convergence. However, the existing results may have limited applicability, since they typically rely on strong conditions on the gradient noise (e.g., an exponentially decaying tail) rather than the more realistic heavy-tailed noise. Unfortunately, when faced with heavy-tailed noise, $\mathtt{SGD}$ is known to exhibit undesirable behavior or even fail to converge. To address the challenge of heavy-tailed noise, people have proposed $\mathtt{Clipped}\text{-}\mathtt{SGD}$, an algorithm that combines $\mathtt{SGD}$ with a simple mechanism, gradient clipping. Although $\mathtt{Clipped}\text{-}\mathtt{SGD}$ performs well in practice, its last-iterate convergence property remains highly underexplored. In this work, we prove the first optimal last-iterate rates in high probability for $\mathtt{Clipped}\text{-}\mathtt{SGD}$ under heavy-tailed noise, thereby closing a gap in the literature.

title: Localized high-Q resonances enable electrically defined beam steering in lithium niobate metasurfaces
abstract: High-speed beam steering for LiDAR and optical communication requires independent, reconfigurable control of optical phase. We demonstrate a metasurface combining lithium niobate's Pockels effect with high-Q (Q > 1700) silicon guided-mode resonance nanoantennas whose localized resonances allow individual electro-optic control at a 1 $μ$m pitch. Identical arrays steer light to 53.5$^\circ$ or 32.4$^\circ$, with the angle set by the bias pattern rather than antenna geometry. We measure 18.0% 0th-order modulation depth, 0.09% of incident power in the steered order, and a 940 MHz detected modulation bandwidth. Mode-overlap analysis shows how inter-element coupling limits usable Q, providing design rules for compact, high-speed beam steering.

title: ACACIAS II: element abundances for 39 stars in the dwarf galaxy Sculptor
abstract: Element abundances in nearby galaxies provide insights into their chemical enrichment histories and place the Milky Way and its neighbours in a broader cosmological context. These systems can be studied through individual stars, whose resolved spectra enable the construction of a chemical abundance census of the Local Group. We present the second stage of the ACACIAS (extra-galactic ArChAeology with Cannon Inferred Abundances from resolved integral field unit Spectra) program, which aims to build the first homogeneous data set of stellar abundances across dwarf galaxies spanning a range of masses for comparison with Milky Way properties. We analyse low-resolution (R=1800), low-SNR (signal-to-noise ratio, ~ 25) MUSE spectra for 39 stars in the Sculptor dwarf spheroidal galaxy. Using the data-driven method The Cannon, we combine high-fidelity labels from the Apache Point Observatory Galactic Evolution Experiment (APOGEE) survey with MUSE-like Large Sky Area Multi-Object Fiber Spectroscopic Telescope (LAMOST) spectra to analyse the MUSE data. This enables the determination of [Mg/Fe], [Mn/Fe], [C/Fe], [N/Fe], and [Al/Fe] on the APOGEE abundance scale, with precisions of σ = 0.09-0.37 dex. Comparing model configurations, we show that [Mg/Fe], [Mn/Fe], and [C/Fe] are best recovered from targeted spectral windows, whereas stellar parameters and [Al/Fe] benefit from full-spectrum information with telluric masking. This reflects the complementary strengths of restricted-window models, which recover abundances from direct spectral features, and full-spectrum models, which exploit correlations with other labels when diagnostic features are weak or absent. Our approach demonstrates the potential of low-resolution, low-SNR stellar spectra to build homogeneous datasets for extragalactic archaeology to better understand the chemical enrichment diversity of the Local Group.

title: SCARCE: Emergent Institutions in Long-Horizon Multi-Agent Coding Systems
abstract: As autonomous agents become widely deployed, coordinating access to shared computing resources and services will become increasingly important. Recent incidents have already revealed unplanned coordination between agents, highlighting the safety implications of these interactions. Yet prior studies of agent negotiation often use stylized games and simulated bargaining, leaving open how these behaviors develop during sustained, long-horizon tasks.
