On 1000 COCO scenes and five small open VLMs (2-5 B parameters), accuracy on a boxed-object identification task falls from near its clean value to chance within a narrow band (half-way visibility V_acc of 12.1-15.9 m in fog and 20.5-38.6 m under water) while, for the four models that are confident on clean images, the confidence stays high: at V=1.95 m in fog their accuracy is at chance but their mean internal confidence is 0.68-0.84 and their verbalized confidence 0.61-1.00, a blind-spot width W=log10(V_acc/V_aware) of at least 0.79 decades, i.e. a factor of 6.2 in visibility. The remaining model is under-confident throughout and its internal confidence follows accuracy. An explicit abstain option follows accuracy when it names the reason (W from -0.21 to -0.06 in fog) but, for one model, lags with a generic "I don't know" (W up to 0.18). ImageNet-C fog severities 1-5 correspond to only 55-110 m of physical visibility, outside the failure band, and leave the accuracy of the models within 5 percentage points of its clean value. Blank-image and shuffled-image controls, a prior-matched answer set and a 200-image pilot that preceded the study are reported. Findings are descriptive: one draw of 1000 images, depth of assumed scale, and models of 2-5 B parameters.

title: UniField++: A Unified Agentic Framework with Loop Reasoning for MRI Field-Strength Enhancement
abstract: MRI field-strength enhancement seeks to combine the accessibility of low-field scanners with the image quality of high-field scanners. Yet, existing methods remain prone to anatomical hallucinations, as uniform processing leaves difficult brain regions insufficiently examined and scarce paired data limit their learning of how tissue contrast and anatomical visibility change across field strengths. To address these challenges, we propose UniField++, a two-agent framework that unifies enhancement tasks across multiple field-strength transitions, including 64mT-to-3T and 3T-to-7T. Unified learning allows both the VLM-based planner and the flow-matching-based enhancer to draw on field-dependent image characteristics observed across tasks, rather than relying on a single transition. Trained with radiologists' annotations of hallucination-prone regions and corresponding correction plans, the planner predicts regional risk and formulates targeted restoration strategies. Guided by these plans, the enhancer performs loop reasoning along the flow-matching trajectory, repeatedly processing high-risk regions for additional refinement. Together, cross-transition learning and risk-guided refinement support anatomically faithful enhancement across field strengths. Across the evaluated tasks, UniField++ improves PSNR by an average of 2.74 dB and SSIM by 14.05 percentage points over comparison methods, with corresponding gains of 3.97 dB and 13.92 percentage points over the ablation baseline. It also maintains enhancement quality on an external cohort with an unseen field strength and improves downstream whole-brain segmentation Macro Dice by an average of 0.1457 over the original low-field images. Code is available at https://github.com/CUHK-AIM-Group/UniField_plusplus.

title: Quantum Tsallis Entropy Estimation: Near-Optimal Bounds and High-Precision Improvements
abstract: Estimating statistical properties of probability distributions is a fundamental problem in statistics and theoretical computer science. We develop quantum algorithms for estimating the $q$-Tsallis entropy $\mathrm{H}_q^{\mathrm{Tsa}}(P) =\frac{\sum_{i=1}^n p_i^q-1}{1-q}$ when $0<q<1$, given purified quantum query access to a distribution $P$ on $[n]$. When $0<q\leq \frac{1}{2}$, we provide a quantum algorithm with query complexity $\widetilde{O}\rbra{\left(\frac{n}{\varepsilon}\right)^{\frac{1}{2q}}}$, which is optimal up to polylogarithmic factors. When $\frac{1}{2}<q<1$, we introduce a two-stage simultaneous probability estimation procedure, yielding a quantum algorithm with query complexity $\widetilde{O}\left(\frac{n^{\frac12+\frac{1}{2q}}}{\varepsilon^{\frac{1}{2q}}}+\frac{n^{1-q}}{\varepsilon}\right)$, which improves the result given by Chen et al. (ICALP 2026) when $\varepsilon=O\rbra{n^{1-2q}}$.

title: Self-Evolving Agents Can Repair Failures but Struggle to Generalize from Them
abstract: Experience-driven self-evolution offers a promising path for large language model (LLM) agents to continually improve through interaction. Yet existing approaches often rely on successful trajectories or external evaluation signals, leaving unclear whether agents can evolve when such positive anchors are unavailable. We study this question through Cold-Start Failure-Only Evolution (CFOE), where agents start without accumulated experience and learn only from failed interactions without privileged guidance. Across three self-evolving paradigms, multiple LLM backbones, and four interactive environments, we uncover a consistent repair-generalization gap: failure-derived experience can help repair previously failed tasks, but rarely yields sustained improvements on unseen tasks. Further analysis shows that agents often misinterpret failures, while even verified-correct experience remains difficult to transfer. Relaxing CFOE reveals that verifier feedback and additional interaction provide limited gains, whereas successful trajectories substantially improve transfer. These findings suggest that current self-evolving agents are better at repairing observed failures than building generalizable capabilities from failure.

title: Prism Attention: Proposal-Refined Index Sharing Mechanism for Efficient LLMs Inference
abstract: Long-context decoding in large language models (LLMs) is increasingly bottlenecked by the memory and computation required to attend over an ever-growing Key-Value (KV) cache at each autoregressive step. Although token-level sparse attention reduces this burden by restricting computation to a small subset of relevant past tokens, its practical gains are often offset by repeatedly recomputing layer-wise sparse indices as the context grows. A common remedy is to share sparse indices across layers by computing them only at designated anchor layers, but such static reuse ignores the layer-wise evolution of attention patterns, causing the reused indices to progressively deviate from the layer-specific optima and incur substantial attention loss. By revisiting cross-layer sparsity from the perspective of attention dynamics, we find that inter-layer salient token shift is highly localized: although the exact top-$κ$ indices differ across layers, the core high-attention tokens remain stable, with changes concentrated near the expanded boundary of previously selected regions. Motivated by this, we propose Prism Attention, a proposal-refined sparse attention framework. It replaces rigid cross-layer index reuse with a coarse-to-fine strategy, preserving layer-wise adaptability while retaining the efficiency benefits of cross-layer sharing. Extensive experiments show that Prism Attention achieves state-of-the-art performance among mainstream sparse attention methods on both reasoning and long-context benchmarks, while attaining a $3.4\times$ end-to-end decoding speedup over FlashAttention at 128K context length.

title: Rigorous verification of period-doubling bifurcations in maps
abstract: We present a computer-assisted approach for proving period-doubling bifurcations in one-parameter families of maps $x \mapsto f(x,λ)$ on $\mathbb{R}^n$. We solve a square augmented system, called the period-doubling map, whose unknowns are the fixed point, the parameter, the right eigenvector attached to the eigenvalue $-1$, the left eigenvector with its eigenvalue, and the vector which describes the center manifold to second order. A contraction argument gives a solution close to a numerical approximation, at which the Jacobian is invertible. The determinant of this Jacobian factors into a simple expression, so that it is nonzero exactly when $1$ is not an eigenvalue and $-1$ is a simple eigenvalue crossing the unit circle transversally. Apart from the sign of the cubic normal-form coefficient, computed afterwards, it remains to check with Gershgorin disks that no other eigenvalue lies on the unit circle. The method is applied to a $10$-mode Galerkin projection of the Kot--Schaffer growth-dispersal model, for which we prove a supercritical period-doubling bifurcation.

title: From Approval to Abuse: Privilege Escalation Attacks on Harness-Protected Coding Agents
abstract: Coding agents use execution harnesses to constrain the consequences of prompt injection by enforcing permission boundaries. These systems deterministically intercept any out-of-sandbox action and prompt the user for approval. To reduce approval fatigue, users can approve allow-rules proposed by the agent, after which any future action matching the rule is allowed without a prompt. In this work, we show that this mechanism introduces a new risk: untrusted context can influence the permissions presented for approval, with consequences extending beyond the immediate task. We investigate privilege escalation targeting this permission-update process. Specifically, adversarial context planted in a repository can reliably steer an agent performing a routine task into requesting a plausibly justified, yet dangerously broad allow-rule. If the user approves the request, the saved rule can effectively blind the harness, enabling adversaries to execute malicious actions that would otherwise require approval, without triggering human oversight. Across production platforms, including Claude Code and Codex CLI, we demonstrate that agents successfully elicit the target allow-rules in 58% of experimental instances. Once acquired, these rules exhibit a massive semantic blast radius, covering 56.9% of category-specific capability test cases. To further quantify the downstream risk, we show that conditional on rule approval, our exploit achieves verified, silent goal completion in 47 of the 58 eligible instances (81.0%), undermining the safety promise of human-in-the-loop oversight.

title: Surprise Masking: Private Data Filtering with Model Likelihoods
abstract: Data useful for language model (LM) training can contain private or unwanted information that is at risk of being learned or memorized. We propose Surprise Masking (SM), a simple form of perplexity filtering that uses a publicly available reference model to identify unwanted spans and suppress learning from them while preserving the rest of each example. On synthetic code benchmarks, we show SM improves the privacy-utility tradeoff over standard masking methods and PII filtering. In fine-tuning experiments, SM reduces approximate extraction of private values from revealed prefixes from 66.3% to 2.3% and the reproduction of stylistic coding quirks from 23.6% to 1.3%, both while preserving performance on the evaluated coding tasks. We also evaluate SM for sanitizing datasets by directly removing unwanted content. Here, SM outperforms DePA, a perplexity-based defense for detecting poisoned dead code, while specialized detectors perform better on broader credential and PII benchmarks. Across eleven settings, we find that SM's downstream success is predictable from the separation of unwanted and useful content in the distribution, and it is particularly useful with code data. Ultimately, SM is an inexpensive, adaptable method to preserve valuable examples while reducing the learning of unwanted information.

title: MUB: An Identity-Masked Benchmark for Music Understanding in Multimodal Language Models
abstract: Evaluating musical perception in multimodal language models requires separating audio evidence from answers recoverable through metadata or external tools. We present the Music Understanding Benchmark (MUB), a locally assembled collection of 500 identity-masked recordings with existing annotations for tempo, key, time signature, and structural intervals. The collection covers all 24 major/minor key combinations, tempos of 47--180 beats per minute, and 4,676 annotated intervals. Original titles, artists, and platform identifiers are excluded from evaluation inputs. Relative to recent music question-answering and temporal-grounding work, MUB emphasizes scalar tempo prediction and full-recording interval outputs, together with a documented metadata-masking protocol. Saved baseline predictions yield 53.6\% tempo accuracy for a simple DSP estimator and 98.4\% time-signature accuracy for a constant 4/4 predictor. We identify important limitations, including an asymmetric legacy key metric, unverified independent annotation agreement, extreme metre imbalance, and unresolved recording-level rights clearance. No contemporary multimodal language model comparison has yet been completed. MUB is therefore an evaluation resource and protocol under validation, rather than a completed demonstration of model capabilities.

title: PersonaCUABench: Benchmarking Computer-Use Agents Serving Diverse Personas
abstract: Computer-use agents (CUAs) are commonly evaluated against fixed task specifications, but users may omit requirements, add constraints, or require approval before consequential actions. Completing the benchmark instruction does not guarantee serving the person who asked. We introduce PersonaCUABench, which holds 74 tasks across 11 domains fixed and varies only who asks. A persona agent, playing one of 44 personas in four groups, rewrites each instruction in that user's own words and answers the CUA's questions, while the CUA sees only the dialogue, never the profile or the original instruction. Across nine backbones (3,330 runs), mean task completion falls by 36% relative to the original requests. The losses have two sources: in 59.9% of cells that lose points, the agent engages with what the user asked for and still gets it wrong, and 11.2% are stops the user requested that the checker scores as failures. Even when a persona request is fully completed, the user gives the top satisfaction rating in only 62.7% of cells, against 84.1% for the original requests. CUAs should therefore be evaluated not only on task completion but also on whether they meet the requirements and constraints users express. Code: https://github.com/MatrAIx-ai/PersonaCUABench. Project page: https://matraix.ai/research/persona-cua.html

title: A100: A Hybrid Vision Foundation Model for Agricultural Plant Image Analysis
abstract: The use of accurate vision models for crop monitoring, disease diagnosis, and plant phenotyping in agriculture is hindered by the lack of expertly annotated data, especially in developing countries. We propose A100, an agricultural vision foundation model that is pre-trained using self-supervised learning on 3 million unlabeled images from fields covering more than 100 crop species. A100 uses a hybrid CNN-Transformer backbone that fuses MBConv stages for local feature extraction with Transformer stages for global contextual representation. A100 uses pre-training with the integration of DINO self-distillation, iBOT masked patch reconstruction, and KoLeo uniformity regularization, resulting in features that are better than ImageNet-12K supervised representations for agricultural applications without any fine-tuning. By utilizing a frozen backbone, the accuracy for crop classification of A100 is 95.37%, which is +2.56% better than ImageNet-12K, and reduces the leaf count error by 10.4% on the GroMo25 phenotyping benchmark, proving that the same backbone can be used for classification and regression tasks. After full fine-tuning, the performance of A100 is 99.90% on 32-class crop identification and 99.02% on 44-class disease detection. On the difficult PlantDoc dataset, A100 outperforms all baselines, such as CvT-13 (64.89% against 63.56%). Remarkably, A100 obtains 98.01% accuracy on plant classification using just 1% of the labelled data (about 284 images per category), showing great label efficiency for use cases with limited labeling. Under an identical protocol, A100 also outperforms the publicly released agricultural foundation models FoMo4Wheat and LeafVision by more than 14 points at 1% labels. We plan to publicly release our pretrained model to allow agricultural professionals to adapt A100 for various plant analysis applications using limited annotations.

title: GOLD: Geometric Optimized Latent Diffusion for Structure-Aware RNA Inverse Folding
abstract: Designing RNA sequences that fold into specific 3D structures is a fundamental challenge in therapeutics. Current RNA inverse folding methods typically condition on 3D backbone coordinates but the generation is limited to 1D discrete sequences. This ignores the continuous side-chain orientations, which are essential for overall structural stability. To address this issue, we explicitly introduce side-chain geometry into the RNA generative process. Unlike co-design frameworks that diffuse across separate raw spaces, we propose Geometric Optimized Latent Diffusion (\textbf{GOLD}), which project sequence and structure into a unified latent manifold. GOLD employs a novel GeoVAE to elegantly integrate discrete RNA sequences with continuous side-chain angles. By mapping these modalities into a single, smooth latent manifold, GOLD naturally facilitates a synergistic co-diffusion process. To enhance structural validity, we further introduce a training-free, gradient-guided sampling mechanism. By decoding the generated sequence probabilities and side-chain geometries into structures during the sampling process, we compute analytical gradients from physical constraints. This dynamic feedback actively guides the generated sequence to a physically stable state. Extensive experiments validate the superiority of GOLD, achieving state-of-the-art performance across sequence recovery, secondary structure validity, and 3D foldability metrics. Our code and data are publicly available at https://github.com/darkflash03/GOLD.

title: Hypergraphs of Low Degree Without Independent Transversals
abstract: For every fixed $k\ge 3$ and every integer $b\ge 2$, we construct a finite vertex-partitioned $k$-uniform hypergraph with blocks of size $b$ and no independent transversal. We show that the maximum number of edges meeting a block is $\left(\frac{(k-1)^{k-1}}{k^k}+O_k(b^{-1})\right)b^k,$ while the maximum vertex degree is $\left(\frac{(k-2)^{k-2}}{(k-1)^{k-1}}+O_k(b^{-1})\right)b^{k-1}$. This shows that the known bound on the number of edges meeting a block is asymptotically sharp even when the leading constant in the maximum vertex degree tends to zero, which answers a problem of Groenland, Kaiser, Treffers, and Wales. By blowing up the same construction, we further obtain for arbitrarily large $n$, there exists a $k$-uniform hypergraph with $n$ blocks, each of size at least $n$, and $Δ(G)<\left(1-\frac1k\right)^{k-1}n^{k-1}$, but with no independent transversal. This gives a negative answer to a problem of Haxell and Wdowinski.

title: Leading-twist proton parton distribution amplitude from scalar and axial-vector diquark correlations
abstract: We compute the leading-twist proton parton distribution amplitude (PDA) using algebraic representations of the nucleon Faddeev wave function inspired by perturbation-theory integral representations. The PDA is obtained from a light-front projection of the covariant quark--diquark Faddeev amplitude and analysed in terms of its scalar- and axial-vector-diquark components. We derive analytic expressions for the corresponding diquark distribution amplitudes and their contributions to the proton PDA. The resulting distribution is broad and concave, with its maximum $(x_1,x_2,x_3)\approx(0.55,0.20,0.25)$ displaced from the symmetric configuration $(1/3,1/3,1/3)$, which corresponds to the maximum of the perturbative-QCD asymptotic form. Scalar-diquark correlations generate a strong asymmetry in the longitudinal momentum distribution, whereas axial-vector correlations redistribute momentum among the valence quarks and significantly reduce this asymmetry. We calculate low-order Mellin moments and obtain a compact parametrisation of the proton PDA at the hadronic scale, $μ_0=0.51\,\mathrm{GeV}$. We then perform the leading-order QCD evolution of its normalized shape to $μ=2\,\mathrm{GeV}$, finding that evolution reduces the momentum asymmetry while preserving a clear imprint of the non-perturbative quark--diquark correlations. The results provide insight into the role of such correlations in shaping the proton light-front structure and furnish non-perturbative input for studies of hard exclusive baryonic processes.

title: Integrated Sensing and Communication in 3GPP: Standardization, Performance Evaluation, and Experimental Validation Toward 6G
abstract: Integrated sensing and communication (ISAC) is evolving from a primarily physical-layer research into a standardized cellular-network capability spanning channel modeling, radio procedures, network architecture, and the delivery of sensing services. We review this progression within the Third Generation Partnership Project (3GPP), from Release 19 service requirements and target-aware channel modeling to the Release 20 New Radio (NR) sensing evaluation framework, radio access network procedures, and system architecture, and discuss future directions toward 6G. We then present two 3GPP-aligned simulation case studies to demonstrate the corresponding evaluation approaches. The first case study compares hard-decision, soft-decision, and hybrid fusion for unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) sensing using multiple transmission and reception points (TRPs). Detection, false alarms, and conditional position and velocity accuracy are evaluated using receiver-derived angle estimates and separately calibrated method-specific thresholds. The second case study compares ideal and practical sensing-assisted predictive handover with conventional handover, while accounting for sensing error and information age. We further present a testbed-based measurement study that characterizes monostatic and bistatic UAV radar cross sections across frequencies, platforms, and observation angles and provides empirical support for correlated target-response modeling. Finally, we discuss open challenges and future research directions in multi-node fusion, resource and interference management, network evolution, security, privacy, and reproducible evaluation. Together, these components connect calibrated channel models, link- and system-level simulation, real-time prototypes, controlled measurements, and field trials through a staged evaluation roadmap.

title: TALLOP: Joint Optimization of Local Training and Communication Compression for Time-Constrained Federated Learning
abstract: Minimizing the wall-clock time required to reach a target accuracy is crucial in federated learning (FL), where many applications require frequent model updates as data distributions evolve over time. Nevertheless, in heterogeneous environments, slow clients with limited computational and communication capabilities can delay global synchronization, forcing faster clients to wait and increasing the overall training time. To mitigate this straggler effect, recent studies have introduced per-round time constraints and adapted client workloads within the available time. However, these approaches primarily focus on local computation, whereas communication can become a major bottleneck in communication-limited environments, motivating the joint optimization of training workload and communication compression. Although previous studies have explored such joint optimization, determining an effective training--communication balance under a fixed per-round time budget remains challenging, as the resulting model performance depends on both training progress and compression-induced degradation. We therefore propose TALLOP, which jointly optimizes the local training workload and communication compression under per-round time constraints. TALLOP predicts the training loss achievable under different computation budgets from the early-stage mini-batch loss trajectory (LENS), and estimates the degradation caused by communication compression using a compression-error model (CLEN). TALLOP combines these predictions to select the training-communication allocation that minimizes the post-compression loss under the given round time constraint. Experiments in heterogeneous FL environments show that TALLOP generally achieves competitive or improved time-to-accuracy compared with approaches that optimize only local training or neither, although the benefit over training-only adaptation depends on the setting.

title: GR-VIP: Geometric representation conditioning for precise visuomotor policy
abstract: Achieving precise terminal position and heading alignment remains a significant challenge for learning-based mobile robot control. Recent vision-based learning methods have shown promise for precise target-relative control and generalization to unseen environments with pretrained visual encoders, but general-purpose visual representations are not specifically designed to capture the fine-grained spatial differences between current and goal views required for precise control, and real-world demonstrations combining millimeter-scale terminal accuracy with zero-shot transfer across environments remain limited. To address these challenges, we propose Geometric Representation Conditioning for Precise Visuomotor Policy (GR-VIP), a goal-conditioned visuomotor policy that leverages a visual encoder pretrained for relative camera pose estimation. Rather than using the final relative-pose estimate, GR-VIP conditions action prediction on the dense relational features produced before pose regression, preserving fine-grained cross-view information for learning corrective actions from demonstrations. We evaluate GR-VIP on a real-world docking task and demonstrate high docking success rates and millimeter-scale terminal accuracy in both the training and unseen environments, without additional training for transfer. Furthermore, supplementary experiments illustrate the policy's ability to align with non-docking targets and complete docking under a tested low-light condition.

title: A Label Noise Robust Algorithm for Graph Data using Neighborhood Label Distribution
abstract: Graph Convolutional Networks (GCNs) have demonstrated exceptional performance on graph-structured data. However, their success heavily relies on the availability of clean labels, an assumption that often fails in real-world scenarios. The learnability of GCNs is intrinsically linked to the neighborhood structure of nodes, making it critical to understand how this structure changes in the presence of label noise. In this work, we investigate how the neighborhood label distribution of a node changes under label noise. We mathematically derive that label noise smooths this distribution, which inherently increases its entropy and severely decreases interclass distinguishability. To address this challenge, we propose Leave-one-out Entropy Node Screening (LENS), an end-to-end framework that identifies noisy nodes by measuring the reduction in neighborhood entropy when a specific node is removed. LENS further incorporates a relabeling mechanism to recover and preserve valuable feature information instead of entirely discarding the identified noisy nodes. Crucially, the end-to-end computational overhead of LENS is remarkably low. Extensive evaluations demonstrate that our algorithm achieves state-of-the-art node classification accuracy while executing an order of magnitude faster than existing noise-robust approaches.

title: Controlling the Diversity-Quality Trade-Off of LLMs by Merging Models Before and After Alignment
abstract: Alignment is known to change the output characteristics of large language models (LLMs). Base models tend to generate more diverse outputs, whereas aligned models tend to produce higher-quality outputs. The appropriate balance between the two depends on the task. Existing methods either require costly fine-tuning or, like temperature sampling, mainly improve lexical diversity rather than semantic diversity. We introduce a depth-aware FrankenMerging approach for controlling the diversity--quality trade-off between an aligned model and its base model without additional training. This approach combines the lower layers of an aligned model with the higher layers of its base model based on the hypothesis that lexical diversity is more closely associated with lower layers and semantic diversity with higher layers. Experiments showed that varying the number of layers taken from each model adjusts both diversity and quality. In most cases, the merged models exhibited higher semantic diversity than the aligned model, and at some split positions, they showed higher lexical diversity than both original models. They also demonstrated a better diversity--quality trade-off than temperature sampling in most settings. A supporting ablation, in which we reversed the merging order, yielded results largely consistent with the hypothesis.

title: Classification of real Lie algebras of dimension one, two and three
abstract: We present an exhaustive, self-contained, and coordinate-free structural classification of real Lie algebras of dimensions one, two, and three up to isomorphism. In dimensions one and two, the classification is governed entirely by the derived ideal and elementary derivation theory. In dimension three, we develop the classical exterior duality isomorphism $Λ^2\mathfrak{g} \cong \mathfrak{g}^* \otimes Λ^3\mathfrak{g}$ pioneered by Bryant and Milnor, which reduces the quadratic Jacobi identity on the $3 \times 3$ structure matrix $C = S + \hat{a}$ to the linear orthogonality relation $S \cdot a = 0$, where $a = \frac{1}{2}χ$ is the trace covector. We systematically bifurcate the three-dimensional category into unimodular ($a = 0$) and non-unimodular ($a \neq 0$) sectors, completely recovering the nine classical Bianchi isomorphism classes (Bianchi types I through IX) alongside their continuous moduli invariants. Furthermore, we establish the Levi--Malcev decomposition for low dimensions, compute the exact minimal representation dimension $μ(\mathfrak{g})$ via Ado's Theorem by constructing explicit matrix realizations in $\mathfrak{gl}(μ, \mathbb{R})$, and formulate a deterministic, coordinate-free decision algorithm for algebra identification.

title: BRICE: Brain-inspired Recurrent Illusory Contour Encoder for Point Cloud Completion
abstract: Mainstream point cloud completion methods are unanimously based on deep learning architectures. On one hand, these methods tend to repetitively stacking attention modules to enhance network performance, which drifts away from the neat design of unified and interpret-able networks; on the other hand, nearly all existing architectures rely solely on feed-forward connections to propagate information, neglecting feedback from deeper layers. The recurrent neural architecture, formed by feedforward-feedback loops, have shown its ability to generate Illusory Contours (ICs) in the V1 brain region of mammals; and ICs are essentially a completion mechanism of the brain for visual information. Motivated by this, we design a Brain-inspired Recurrent Illusory Contour Encoder (BRICE) to "imagine" what is missing in the incomplete 3D point clouds. Building upon the foundation model of Predictive Coding (PC), the plug-and-play nature enables BRICE to be seamlessly integrated into mainstream point cloud completion baselines. Experimental results show that BRICE can enhance various completion baselines on different 3D datasets such as MVP2K, PCN, and PlantPCom. Our code: Https://github.com/wangyunlei-wyl/BRICE.

title: Robotic Spatiotemporal Editing: A Unified Interface for Controllable Action Generation via Masked Action Reconstruction
abstract: Generative policies can synthesize robot behaviors, yet controlling and editing them through diverse spatiotemporal references remains challenging. In the real world, human intent requires robot behaviors that satisfy constraints on where, when, and how actions are executed. Our key insight is that spatiotemporal control references, such as keypoints, flows, orientations, and keyposes, can be viewed as partial specifications of the same temporal Cartesian action space. We introduce the MAP (Masked Action Space) interface to unify these action references and formulate controllable manipulation as an action inpainting problem. Our Inpainting Policy (IP) reconstructs missing action dimensions of the end-effector, combining progress-guided alignment with multi-mask training to support unseen action-constraint combinations. We further adopt a training-free RePaint variant that iteratively inpaints the action during denoising to reduce control error. On ManiSkill and LIBERO-10, our policy achieves average task success rates of 92.67% and 64.67%, respectively.Real-world experiments demonstrate spatiotemporal control with average positional and rotational errors of 44.3 mm and 7°, respectively, showing that our policy can use diverse references to guide executable robot behaviors.

title: Perron-Wright asymptotics and critical component processes for regular inhomogeneous random graphs
abstract: We extend Wright's enumeration of connected labelled graphs with fixed surplus to irreducible critical finite type kernels and regular compact type kernels. Let $C_t(k,r)$ denote the total weight of connected labelled graphs with $k$ vertices and surplus $r$. Let $u>0$ satisfy $Ku=u$ and $\int u\,dμ=1$, and put $α=\int u^2\,dμ$ and $β=\int u^3\,dμ$. We prove that the rooted-tree radius $ρ$ is positive and real analytic near $1$, with $ρ(1)=1$ and $\logρ(t)=\frac{α^2}{2β}(t-1)^2+O(|t-1|^3)$, and that, for fixed $r\in\mathbb{Z}_{\ge0}$ and $0\le L < \infty$, $C_t(k,r)=w_rβ^{(r-1)/2}e^{-k}ρ(t)^{-k}k^{k+3r/2-2}\{1+O_{r,L}(k^{-1/2})\}$, uniformly for $|t-1|\le Lk^{-1/2}$, where $w_r$ is the classical Wright constant. At $t_n=1+λn^{-1/3}$, these asymptotics yield local size and surplus point-process limits for deterministic finite type models and annealed compact type Bollobas-Janson-Riordan models satisfying projective quadratic regularity. After rescaling component sizes by $β^{1/3}n^{-2/3}$, the limit is the Aldous process at parameter $αβ^{-2/3}λ$, and the corresponding type profiles concentrate at the Perron law $p(dx)=u(x)μ(dx)$. For every regular countable critical kernel, we construct graph sequences with growing finite supports and the same local limits, and identify the additive shift of the critical window caused by spectral perturbations of order $n^{-1/3}$.

title: A cubulation of the associahedron using a torus-equivariant degeneration of the brick variety
abstract: We describe a mixed subdivision of the $(n-1)$-dimensional Loday associahedron into $(n-1)!$ maximal cells which are combinatorial cubes, and we show that the face poset of this subdivision is isomorphic to the face poset of the subdivision of the $1\times 2\times \dotsb \times (n-1)$ box into unit cubes. More generally, we describe mixed subdivisions of generalized associahedra into pieces which are Minkowski sums of Bruhat interval polytopes. Our subdivisions arise from a torus-equivariant embedded (in a product of flag varieties) degeneration of brick varieties into reduced unions of products of Richardson varieties. The subdivision of Loday's associahedron allows us to `embed' the 1-skeleton of the permutahedron in the boundary of the associahedron.

title: Low-Cost Third-order Algebraic Diagrammatic Construction Method for Excited States Using Tensor Hypercontraction and State-Specific Frozen Natural Orbitals
abstract: We have developed a reduced-cost framework for excited-state calculations by combining the state-specific frozen natural orbital (SS-FNO) approach with the third-order algebraic diagrammatic construction [ADC(3)] method and tensor hypercontraction (THC). This strategy enables a systematic and controllable truncation of the virtual orbital space, while significantly lowering the computational scaling through the THC representation of the electron repulsion integrals. The method allows black-box application via adjustable thresholds and includes a perturbative correction that compensates for the truncation error. We have used the CIS(D) method to generate the natural orbitals for the excited states. The performance of the SS-FNO-THC-ADC(3) method is assessed for valence, Rydberg, and charge-transfer excitations. Benchmark calculations demonstrate that the combined approach achieves excellent agreement with the canonical ADC(3) results. The efficiency of the present implementation is demonstrated by calculating the excitation energy of a molecule containing 31 atoms and more than one thousand basis functions.

title: Efficient CPU-GPU collaborative MoE inference via Adaptive Expert Assignment
abstract: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models reduce inference computation through sparse expert activation, but their large expert memory footprint often exceeds GPU capacity, making expert offloading necessary for memory-constrained inference. However, existing systems typically handle GPU-missed experts by either transferring them to the GPU, incurring substantial PCIe transfer latency, or executing them on the CPU, making the slower CPU computation the bottleneck. To address these limitations, we present \method, a CPU-GPU collaborative MoE inference system that adaptively assigns these missed experts to the CPU or GPU for efficient execution. By exploiting differences in expert token-loads, \method selectively transfers high-load experts to the GPU while executing low-load experts on the CPU. To minimize inference latency, \method adaptively adjusts expert assignments to balance the CPU computation path against the GPU transfer-and-computation path, allowing both execution paths to complete as early as possible. Extensive experiments on three representative MoE LLMs show that \method improves prefill speed by up to 51.9\% and decode throughput by up to 39.5\% over the strongest baseline across the evaluated batch sizes, with consistent gains under different GPU-memory budgets.

title: A Minimal ReLU Classifier on Non-Linearly Separable Data: Convergence and Implicit Bias at and beyond the Edge of Stability
abstract: Gradient descent (GD) with large learning rates can successfully optimize neural networks even though classical smoothness-based learning rate conditions are violated. Yet theory for this regime largely covers linear models or linearly separable data. We analyze a minimal setting outside both regimes. Specifically, a two-neuron ReLU network trained with logistic loss on 1D non-linearly separable data. The objective is nonconvex and nonsmooth, and GD exhibits edge-of-stability (EoS) behavior. We identify an active cone in parameter space that contains every perfect classifier, where the problem becomes piecewise logistic regression with a varying effective dataset. Within this cone, we prove a finite-time loss bound for constant learning rates and show that GD converges in direction to an explicit max-margin vector, while the orthogonal component converges to the unique minimizer of a non-strongly convex potential. We further establish catapult results where exponentially small loss is reached after a single loss spike. Furthermore, we propose an adaptive schedule that lets learning rates grow to infinity without leaving the active cone. We prove that this schedule achieves a loss rate of $O(1/(T\log{T})$, which is faster than the standard $O(1/T)$ rate. Our theoretical results extend to local convergence on more general network and are validated on MNIST dataset. Overall, we show that this setup provides a tractable neural-network model for studying large and adaptive step sizes beyond linear predictors and separable data.

title: Classification of real Lie algebras of dimension four
abstract: We present an exhaustive, coordinate-free, and self-contained classification of four-dimensional real Lie algebras up to isomorphism. In dimension three, classification schemes frequently exploit Bryant's classical exterior duality isomorphism $Λ^2\mathfrak{g} \cong \mathfrak{g}^* \otimes Λ^3\mathfrak{g}$, which reduces the Jacobi identity to an elegant linear algebraic condition on a single $3\times 3$ matrix. We explicitly demonstrate that this accidental isomorphism breaks down in dimension four due to the dimensional mismatch $\dim Λ^2\mathfrak{g} = 6 \neq 4 = \dim(\mathfrak{g}^* \otimes Λ^4\mathfrak{g})$, transforming the Jacobi identity into a non-linear system of 16 quadratic constraints on 24 structure constants. To overcome this geometric obstruction without relying on brute-force polynomial elimination, we employ an intrinsic Lie-theoretic reduction: the Levi--Malcev decomposition isolates the non-solvable sector into direct products with three-dimensional simple ideals, while the solvable sector is classified by anchoring the structure to its nilradical $\mathfrak{n}$, which is an intrinsic characteristic ideal. For codimension-one nilradicals ($\dim\mathfrak{n} = 3$), the problem is reduced to classifying outer derivations of $\mathbb{R}^3$ and the Heisenberg algebra $\mathfrak{h}_3$ under the action of the automorphism group modulo global rescaling and central translations. For two-dimensional nilradicals, the structure is resolved via maximal abelian sub-algebras of $\mathfrak{gl}(2,\mathbb{R})$ lacking nilpotent elements. Complete proofs are supplied for all reductions, precise moduli parameter ranges are established to eliminate redundancies, and an explicit isomorphism dictionary is provided bridging our structural models with classical tabulations in mathematical physics.

title: "Deep lifts": Neural networks can generalize even with the dumbest optimizer
abstract: Given a labeled dataset $\{(x_i, y_i)\}_{i = 1}^n$, consider drawing a parameter vector $\hatθ$ uniformly at random from those that interpolate the data within a width-$W$ depth-$D$ ReLU architecture with continuous weights bounded within $[-M, M]$. We study the generalization properties of $\hatθ$ in the case where the dataset can, in fact, be explained by a smaller $w$-by-$d$ ReLU network. Despite the obliviousness of the selection rule for $\hatθ$, it adaptively generalizes at the rate $\tilde O\left(\frac{wdWD}{n}\right)$, rather than being governed by the VC dimension of the full $W$-by-$D$ hypothesis class. The reason is due to a particular inductive bias in ReLU networks: the $w$-by-$d$ parameter *witnesses* an exponential volume of $W$-by-$D$ interpolating parameters, which dwarfs the volume of poorly generalizing parameters (conditioned on interpolation). We explicitly construct this set of near-equivalent $W$-by-$D$ parameters by a proof technique called *deep lifting*, and then tie the achievable volume to stability properties of the $w$-by-$d$ witness. Examples show that these techniques allow us to convert approximation-theoretic results into generalization guarantees for nonparametric classes. We further show that generalization of uniform-random interpolators can survive label corruptions.

title: What Makes a Good Symbol for Hybrid Discrete-Continuous Planning?
abstract: The physical world has continuous state and action spaces, yet robot planning often benefits from hybrid discrete-continuous formulations that explicitly expose combinatorial structure, such as contact modes or discrete primitive actions. Existing methods typically rely on human-defined symbol sets or symbols derived from language supervision, without asking what makes a symbol computationally useful. In this paper, we take an inference-algorithm--centric view to define usefulness: a good symbol should expose the discrete commitments that simplify solving the original planning problem. We first introduce the concept of solver-sufficient symbolization by studying finite-horizon piecewise-affine systems, for which solver sufficiency can be precisely characterized, and develop a counterexample-guided algorithm for symbol invention. We then extend this principle to invent symbols for optimization objectives parameterized by general neural networks as energy functions, showing that solver-sufficient symbols can nevertheless be induced from their continuous optimization landscapes. Experiments on simulated and real-robot tasks show that the resulting symbols reduce solving cost while preserving solution quality, while also improving interpretability and steerability. Furthermore, our theoretical and algorithmic insights help explain why certain human-defined symbols are computationally useful.

title: Spectral Schwarz Lemmas and Parallel Obstructions to Metric Comparison
abstract: In this paper, we characterize when comparison of contracted Chern curvatures implies comparison of Hermitian bundle metrics with the same constant on compact Hermitian bases. If the curvature contraction of the reference metric is semipositive, this implication holds for every Hermitian metric if and only if the kernel of this contraction contains no nonzero subbundle parallel with respect to the Chern connection of the reference metric. The equality terms of a $C^2$ spectral truncation identify the parallel summand on which comparison can fail, without regularity assumptions on the curvature kernel. We also establish a sharp operator estimate, with a constant independent of the bundle ranks, for holomorphic bundle maps on complete Kähler bases under curvature bounds and bounded base-map energy density. Smooth Schatten moments give global control without a separate boundedness assumption on the bundle map. Finally, we obtain rank bounds and conditions for vanishing on compact Hermitian bases from directional curvature traces over fiber subspaces. For higher-dimensional subspaces, these conditions allow mixed signs on individual fiber lines.

title: Adaptation of Computer Use Agents to New Software with User Manuals
abstract: Recent advances in multimodal foundation models have significantly improved the ability to operate real-world software through graphical user interfaces (GUIs) using visual observations and natural language instructions. However, maintaining strong performance on unseen applications remains challenging, as practical tasks often require long-horizon procedural knowledge and application-specific operation patterns. In addition, constructing executable tasks and collecting corresponding trajectories for training still heavily rely on human-annotated data, incurring substantial cost. In this paper, we propose MAGE (Manual-augmented computer use AGent Execution and learning), a framework that leverages user manuals as a scalable source of procedural knowledge to improve both inference and training. During execution, MAGE retrieves task-relevant manual content and uses a planner to generate explicit procedural guidance for CUAs. To further account for the discrepancies between manuals and actual GUI environments, such as version differences or user settings, MAGE also adapts the agent policy through environment interaction. During training, MAGE converts manuals into executable task-plan pairs and uses the plans to guide environment rollouts toward task-relevant states; the resulting trajectories are then used to optimize the policy without human-authored demonstrations. This unified design enables effective utilization of manuals for both task execution and training, reducing reliance on human-authored training data. Experimental results across six applications demonstrate improvements in task success rates over strong baselines, highlighting the effectiveness of manual-guided planning and policy adaptation in new software environments. We provide the code and reproduction scripts at https://github.com/ku-autoai/MAGE.

title: Transport Signatures of a Kinetically Self-Trapped Nagaoka Polaron
abstract: Nagaoka polarons are canonical examples of kinetic magnetism. Although their spin structure is well understood, their transport remains unexplored. We compute the dynamical mobility of a single hole in the square-lattice $t$-model using resummation-based quantum Monte Carlo and analytic continuation. Upon cooling, an incoherent Drude-like response gives way to a finite-frequency peak as the dc mobility vanishes. The peak signals an internal mode of a hole confined by its ferromagnetic cloud. Our results establish transport as an incisive probe of polaron formation and kinetic self-trapping.

title: QuarkShard: Decomposing Cross-Shard Requests into Single-Input Transactions
abstract: Sharding blockchains enhance scalability by distributing the workload across multiple shards. Within sharding blockchains, securely and efficiently processing cross-shard user requests remains a pivotal challenge. Traditional sharding blockchain protocols execute cross-shard requests under a processing paradigm that treats each user request as a monolithic entity to preserve its atomicity, inherently introducing significant intra-shard BFT execution overhead and cross-shard communication overhead. We propose QuarkShard, a sharding protocol that breaks away from this traditional paradigm to achieve intra-shard and cross-shard overheads below the lower bounds imposed by conventional approaches. QuarkShard decomposes cross-shard requests into single-input-shard transactions, where each transaction requires consensus and processing within only a single shard, thereby substantially reducing total request processing overhead. Meanwhile, through a carefully designed request decomposition algorithm, QuarkShard guarantees fund atomicity or location atomicity during request execution. QuarkShard also enhances the security of blockchain sharding systems against MEV attacks and flooding attacks. Empirical evaluation across a wide-area network spanning four AWS regions demonstrates that QuarkShard achieves superior performance, attaining a peak throughput of $1024$k requests per second with sub-$4$-second latency. Benchmark comparisons show that QuarkShard achieves up to $210.7\%$ and $314.8\%$ of the maximum throughputs of Kronos and 2PC, respectively.

title: Crystal Field-Phonon Coupling in ErFeO$_3$ Single Crystal Via Inelastic Neutron Scattering
abstract: Crystal-field (CF) excitations and their coupling to lattice vibrations were investigated in ErFeO$_3$ using inelastic neutron scattering. Pronounced modifications of the excitation spectra, including energy shifts, intensity redistribution, and linewidth changes, were observed as a consequence of CF-phonon coupling. Significant renormalization of the first and second CF excitations, located near 5 meV and 12 meV, respectively, was detected along both transverse and longitudinal directions in the vicinity of the reciprocal-space point Q = (2, 0, 4). The coupling effects become more prominent as the temperature increases from 300 K to 650 K, while a slight suppression is observed at 750 K. Remarkably, CF excitation peaks that are strongly weakened by thermal population effects re-emerge in specific momentum regions through interaction with phonon modes. The coupled excitations exhibit characteristic signatures of hybridization, including energy renormalization, intensity enhancement, and linewidth narrowing. Density-functional-theory-based phonon calculations further support the interpretation of CF-phonon coupling in ErFeO3. These results demonstrate that strong interactions between CF excitations and lattice vibrations can substantially modify the excitation spectra in rare-earth orthoferrites.

title: How bright can a galaxy be? Extreme value predictions for high-redshift survey observables
abstract: Assessing the significance of extreme galaxy candidates has typically relied on redshifts and stellar / halo masses inferred through inverse modelling, which carries substantial systematic uncertainty. We combine the halo mass function with a conditional model for galaxy emission and apply the Extreme Value Statistics (EVS) formalism to predict the distribution of the observed flux of the brightest galaxy expected in a given survey area, redshift interval and photometric band. We find the choice of parametric star formation history (SFH) dominates the modelling uncertainty, introducing a spread approaching $\sim 1 \, \mathrm{dex}$ by $z \sim 18$, whilst the stellar population synthesis model, initial mass function and metallicity each contribute $\lesssim 0.3 \, \mathrm{dex}$. The luminous $z \gtrsim 9$ candidates in COSMOS-Web cluster about the median prediction for the area they were drawn from, and lie at least an order of magnitude below the $3σ$ limit, a margin comparable to the SFH systematic. Of the observational samples reaching beyond $z \sim 13$, the two spectroscopically confirmed galaxies at $z \simeq 14$ lie close to the median prediction for their area, whereas photometric candidates at $z \gtrsim 16$ reach $+4σ$ (a probability to exceed of $\sim 10^{-5}$), the brightest lying at the limit obtained by converting all halo baryons into stars. Since the prediction bounds the flux far more tightly than the photometry bounds the redshift, such offsets are most naturally resolved by errors in the inferred redshifts. This approach allows extreme candidates to be assessed directly in the observational plane, making explicit the modelling assumptions common to forward and inverse approaches.

title: Diffusion-controlled reactions with time-dependent surface reactivity
abstract: We investigate diffusion-controlled reactions on a reactive surface with time-dependent reactivity. Starting from a conventional formulation via diffusion equation with Robin boundary condition for the macroscopic concentration of particles, we aim at quantifying how temporal variations of reactivity affect the survival probability and the associated first-reaction time (FRT) of a single particle on the reactive surface. Using an adiabatic description, we first identify five long-time regimes of the first-reaction time distribution, ranging from exponential and stretched-exponential to power-law decay. In particular, sufficiently rapid decay of the reactivity leads to a nonzero probability of never reacting, despite diffusion in a bounded domain. Second, we provide a probabilistic reformulation of this problem and compare it with a different scenario of encounter-dependent reactivity. Our theoretical predictions are validated via extensive Monte Carlo simulations.

title: VLA-Fabric: Learning Interaction for Composable Multi-Arm VLA Agents
abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models are rapidly expanding what individual robots can accomplish, yet many real-world manipulation settings require multiple arms to operate as a coordinated system. Existing approaches organize multi-arm coordination in different ways, including centralized joint policies, high-level task or role assignment, and locally executed policies that react to teammates. However, how complete action-producing VLAs should explicitly interact with one another during action generation remains largely unexplored. We introduce VLA-Fabric, which organizes one complete VLA per arm while preserving local perception and action ownership, and enables coordination through learned interaction across policy boundaries. We first systematically study where such interaction should occur, how peer information should be aggregated, and how the interaction should be learned, revealing complementary coordination functions spanning shared context, peer-specific latent information, and action-stage interaction. We then re-instantiate these functions in a structurally different VLA architecture, showing that the coordination principle is not tied to a particular tensor layout or backbone implementation. Finally, we compose teams of three and four arms and evaluate them in simulation and physical experiments. On all four physical tasks, Full interaction improves success over independently trained local policies by 16--40 percentage points. Together, these results suggest that explicit interaction among complete VLA policies offers a scalable path toward networked embodied intelligence.

title: PASS: A Trustworthy Precision Approach Simulation System for CAT III Integrity Algorithm Development
abstract: For fixed-wing aircraft, reliable localization during approach and landing is critical to flight safety. Visual--inertial navigation is promising, but aircraft navigation also requires integrity: trustworthy outputs and timely warnings when they should not be used. Real approach data are costly to collect, while many visual errors and failures required for integrity algorithm development are difficult to reproduce safely. We present PASS, a trustworthy Precision Approach Simulation System for CAT III integrity algorithm development. In a unified temporal and geometric framework, PASS integrates configurable airport environments, prescribed trajectories, inertial simulation, calibrated stereo images, and continuous runway-relative ground truth. It supports navigation and integrity research through controllable sensor errors and environmental variations, computable visual projection errors, deterministic runway geometry priors, and condition-labeled data for statistical error modeling. We further propose Sim-to-Real Scene Trustworthiness (SRST), a measure based on DINOv2 feature distributions and UMAP, to quantify sim-to-real closeness. Experiments with representative stereo--inertial estimators demonstrate the usability of the generated sequences and quantify localization errors across algorithms and environments. PASS provides a controllable foundation for developing and evaluating visual--inertial navigation and integrity algorithms for fixed-wing precision approaches up to CAT III requirements.

title: Hemicompactness and the $k_ω$-property of free topological vector spaces
abstract: For a Tychonoff space $X$ we consider the vector space $E(X)$ with basis $X$ endowed with one of the following topologies: the weak topologies $L_b(X)$ and $L_p(X)$ generated by $C_b(X)$ and $C(X)$, the free locally convex space $L(X)$, the free locally $r$-convex space $L^{(r)}(X)$ ($0<r\le1$), the free locally pseudoconvex space $L^{(0)}(X)$, and the free topological vector space $V(X)$. We prove that $L_b(X)$ is hemicompact if and only if $X$ is finite; that for every vector topology between $L_p(X)$ and $L^{(0)}(X)$ hemicompactness is equivalent to $X$ being countable with all compact subsets finite; and that $V(X)$, as well as the free topological groups $F(X)$ and $A(X)$, are hemicompact if and only if $X$ is hemicompact. In particular, $V([0,1])$ is hemicompact, while $L([0,1])$ and $L_p([0,1])$ are not. We also describe when these spaces are $k_ω$-spaces: $L_b(X)$ and $L_p(X)$ only for finite $X$, and $L^{(r)}(X)$, $0\le r\le1$, only for countable discrete $X$.

title: Semantic-Critical Regions for Video-to-Audio Generation
abstract: In real-world videos, sound events are often associated with localized and fine-grained visual cues, such as object motion, object-part dynamics, contact events, and interactions between objects. Existing video-to-audio (V2A) methods employ implicit conditioning based on global visual representations or explicit control derived from temporal and spatial cues. However, subtle sound-producing and sound-indicative interactions remain insufficiently captured, leaving room for more precise visual conditioning of sound-event semantics and temporal dynamics. Motivated by this observation, we refer to regions containing such sound-relevant visual evidence as Semantic-Critical Regions (SCRs) and introduce SCR-V2A, a V2A generation framework that explicitly localizes and encodes SCRs as fine-grained visual guidance for audio generation. Specifically, we first identify SCRs through sound-related visual localization. We then transform the localized regions into a control representation through adapter-based dual visual encoding, which jointly captures global visual context and fine-grained sound-relevant evidence. The representation is used to condition a downstream audio generation model. Experiments on both in-domain and out-of-domain benchmarks demonstrate that SCR-V2A achieves strong performance in distribution matching and audio quality while remaining competitive in cross-modal alignment and requiring few trainable parameters. These results highlight the value of prioritizing fine-grained, sound-relevant visual regions for V2A generation.

title: Stochastic Shockwave Dynamics in First-Order Traffic Flow
abstract: Moving congestion fronts vary across realizations even when the traffic-flow law is fixed. This paper develops a generator-based formulation of the Lighthill--Whitham--Richards (LWR) model with random initial density and a deterministic fundamental diagram. Randomness enters through the initial spatial density field; every realization follows the same conservation law. For a smooth strictly concave fundamental diagram, we adapt established one-sided spatial Markov closure to traffic variables under the stated spatial-process and regularity assumptions, and derive a kinetic balance for physically normalized front intensities. Evolving the spatial generator provides density laws and congestion-front statistics without solving a road-grid problem for every realization. The formulation is continuous in physical space and time, while its numerical implementation approximates density state and integrates physical time. Four experiments distinguish deterministic consistency from stochastic comparison. Riemann and signal examples recover independently constructed exact LWR solutions. Smooth strictly concave approximations approach the deterministic triangular-diagram signal solution over the tested finite horizons; this does not establish stochastic closure at contacts or the capacity kink. A matched Monte Carlo Godunov ensemble evaluates front counts, sizes, mergers, and density distributions. The evolved generator also yields an instantaneous travel-time distribution for a frozen density field, compared with the same functional of the matched Godunov profiles. This quantity is not experienced travel time through evolving traffic. Resolution checks identify remaining normalization and small-front-loss effects. The contribution is direct evolution and interpretation of traffic-state and front distributions under a fixed first-order traffic law.

title: Arbitrary Functors as Modalities in a Linear Calculus
abstract: We study modalities in the linear lambda calculus, by interpreting them as endofunctors in monoidal closed categories. We support functors that do not distribute over products, including (co)monads. We also support arbitrary natural transformations as conversion between modalities. We provide a generic categorical semantics, which we then specialise to a sound and complete resource semantics. We use this resource semantics to derive normalisation by evaluation. Along the way, we describe several applications of such models. This work aims at providing a foundation for future programming languages with modalities. The paper is backed by a mechanisation in Agda.

title: The geometric exceptional set for Fano threefolds
abstract: We study the geometric exceptional set in Manin's conjecture for smooth Fano threefolds. We prove that every adjoint rigid surface with $a$-invariant one on a non-product smooth Fano threefold is normal. This yields a description of the geometric exceptional set in terms of the higher-$a$ locus, anticanonical conics, and del Pezzo fibrations. Zariski density arise only from the latter two contributions. For del Pezzo fibrations, we construct a finite collection of parameter covers which controlling the associated breaking maps. We classify their low-genus components for general smooth Fano threefolds yielding examples with potentially Zariski dense geometric exceptional sets in $22$ of the $105$ deformation families. Extending Batyrev-Tschinkel's example, we construct Fano fourfolds with quartic del Pezzo fibrations and an explicit Fano threefold with two degree-six del Pezzo fibrations, all with Zariski dense geometric exceptional sets. For this threefold, the original form of Manin's conjecture fails on every non-empty open subset for every anticanonical height.

title: Causal Value Attribution of Marketing Labels in LLM-Generated Ads: A Deconfounder Approach
abstract: As AI-generated content becomes commoditized, economic value increasingly shifts from final artifacts to the upstream expertise used to specify inputs that steer LLM generation. Yet organizations lack methods for valuing this expertise and identifying which individual skills or configurations causally improve performance. This study examines generative marketing, where structured expert labels serve as skill primitives conditioning LLM-generated advertisements. Estimating their causal effects is difficult because outcomes reflect stochastic LLM mediation, high-dimensional label interactions, and multimodal confounding. This study proposes D-VAE (Deconfounder Variational Autoencoder), a counterfactual-inference framework integrating a multi-treatment deconfounder with causal representation learning. D-VAE recovers causally disentangled expert-labeling logic and derives PAC-based bounds on omitted-variable bias from single-treatment confounders. Applied to 29,177 foundation-makeup ad creatives, D-VAE outperforms state-of-the-art benchmarks. A field experiment shows that recommended configurations increase engagement by 32.7% and perform statistically indistinguishably from human experts, while a simulation study confirms causal attribution under complex confounding and treatment interactions. Overall, the study shifts value assessment from AI-generated products to skills, providing a foundation for pricing and optimizing AI-augmented skill portfolios.

title: An Efficient Blind Detection of OFDM Signals with Unknown Parameters
abstract: This study investigates efficient detector designs for the blind detection of orthogonal frequency-division multiplexing (OFDM) signals with unknown power, bandwidth, and carrier frequency in wideband spectrum sensing. We first describe the received signal model and conduct an asymptotic covariance analysis to obtain a tractable discrete-time representation. Based on this model, generalized likelihood ratio test (GLRT) detectors are derived for both known and unknown noise power cases in a single-antenna receiver setting. The proposed framework is subsequently extended to multi-antenna receivers, and the corresponding multi-antenna GLRT detectors are developed for both known and unknown noise power cases. Importantly, using the cumulative-sum (CUSUM) operations, the resulting detectors reduce to an efficient one-dimensional (1D) search in both single-antenna and multi-antenna settings. We also provide theoretical analysis for the conventional energy detector (Conv-ED) and the hypothetical uniformly most powerful (UMP) test to reveal the impact of system parameters on detection performance. In addition, computational complexity analysis is presented for both the proposed and conventional detectors. Finally, comprehensive simulation results are provided to evaluate the probability of detection. The results demonstrate that the proposed detectors achieve performance close to that of a genie-aided detector while significantly outperforming conventional detection approaches.

title: ASE: Attribution-Guided Semantic Evolution for Time Series Forecasting
abstract: External text can supply predictive information absent from numerical histories, but its value depends on how it is represented, combined and deployed. We present Attribution-guided Semantic Evolution (ASE), a modular framework for constructing textual factors, evaluating their conditional contribution, and deploying validation-selected numerical--textual predictors. ASE supports task-specific implementations with lexical measurements, semantic primitives or evolved event/state factors, coupled to suitable numerical experts. Its feedback-based implementation uses conditional refitting diagnostics to guide factor revision and combination search. We evaluate ASE on the four text-associated TESS datasets and dynamic CSI 300 stock ranking. The four forecasting implementations obtain test MSEs of 0.001041, 0.022439, 0.333115 and 1.8150, each below the corresponding published TESS score. On CSI 300, the frozen text-fusion implementation improves mean RankIC by 0.000642 over its numerical expert and by 0.000701 over matched shuffled text, with positive differences in all five seeds. Controlled text perturbations support functional reliance on text correspondence, while incumbent retention prevents regressions in the measured development criterion. Together, the experiments characterize ASE at two levels: forecasting performance of task-specific implementations and the conditional contributions of individual modules.

title: Gamma-ray calorimetry of Seyfert winds
abstract: Two stacking analyses with the Fermi Large Area Telescope (LAT) detected GeV emission from radio-quiet Seyferts, one selected by an X-ray ultra-fast outflow (UFO) and one hard-X-ray-bright, with similar luminosities attributed to different mechanisms: wind shocks and the accretion-disk corona. We investigate how efficiently Seyfert outflows convert mechanical power into GeV photons, whether the two detections require distinct mechanisms, and how Seyferts compare with low-ionization nuclear emission-line regions (LINERs). Without new Fermi-LAT data reduction, we homogenize published measurements to 0.1-100 GeV, place local mechanical accelerators on one L_gamma-Edot diagram, and express eta = L_gamma/Edot as a fraction rho of the complete-calorimetry efficiency eta_max ~ 2.5%, inverting rho for the ambient density required by pp losses. Winds from Seyfert active galactic nuclei (AGN) have rho = 0.020 (+0.018/-0.011) for acceleration efficiency 0.1, a factor of ~13.5 below starburst superwinds (rho = 0.26 (+0.37/-0.16)). The difference exceeds a factor of three with probability 0.95 and is independent of acceleration parameters common to both classes; it is conditional on the wind kinetic powers, collapsing only if every wind sits at its minimum launch radius. The implied densities, ~10 and ~100 cm^-3, are consistency values: density, shock radius and speed are degenerate. The two stacking detections agree within a factor of 1.75 in gamma-ray output per unit Eddington luminosity, but the 95% interval, 0.26-24, is too wide to distinguish them. A third stack, of 186 low-luminosity AGN, extends the comparison 1.5 dex lower, ordered by AGN power. GeV detectability of non-jetted AGN is set by the product of mechanical power and calorimetric fraction. LINER outflows fail on power; for the adopted wind energetics, Seyfert UFO winds fail on calorimetry; starburst superwinds succeed on both.

title: Liouville theorems for $-Δ_{m,g}u=λe^u|\nabla u|^q$ in the full range of gradient exponents
abstract: We study the equation \[ -Δ_{m,g}u=λe^u|\nabla u|^q \] on complete, connected, noncompact Riemannian manifolds of dimension $n\ge2$ with $\Ric_g\ge0$. For every $m>1$, $q\in\mathbb R$ and $λ>0$, we prove that every positive $C^1$ weak solution is constant when $q>0$, while no such solution exists when $q\le0$. For $q>m$, we derive a local gradient estimate independent of the solution by Nash--Moser iteration, which leads to automatic boundedness and resolves the question raised by Lu and Zhu~\cite[Remark~1.6(B)]{LZ}. For $m-1<q<m$, we use an auxiliary function and a divergence inequality to extend the Liouville result beyond the range covered by existing gradient-inequality methods. The remaining cases are treated by suitable changes of variables and integral estimates. The conclusions also extend to real-valued solutions bounded below.

title: ECHO: Replacing the Compliance Proxy with Response Harmfulness in Optimization-Based Jailbreak Attack
abstract: Despite extensive safety alignment, large language models remain vulnerable to jailbreak attacks. Existing optimization-based attacks share a single objective: maximize a token-level proxy of victim compliance---such as the likelihood of an affirmative prefix---computed on the prompt rather than the decoded reply. This proxy cannot distinguish a cautious hedge from a fully actionable harmful answer, leaving the search blind to what the model actually says. We propose ECHO (Evaluation-Conditioned Harmfulness Optimization), which replaces the compliance proxy with response-level, continuous harmfulness scores from HarmSig, a 1.7B regressor grounded in actual harmful capability. ECHO couples HarmSig with five word-level perturbation operators and Keyword-Anchored Beam Search with global top-m memory, under a strict black-box threat model. Across five open-weight victims on AdvBench, ECHO achieves up to 0.898 StrongREJECT mean score and 89.23% HarmBench success. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/STANWYW/echo.

title: Stieltjes-generated moment functionals and orthogonality: a transfer principle and an image theorem
abstract: We study the orthogonality induced by Stieltjes derivatives from the point of view of ordinary polynomial moment functionals. If \(g\) is a derivator and the Stieltjes monomials \(g_{x_0,n}\) are linearly independent, the map \(Φ(t^n)=g_{x_0,n}\) is an isomorphism of differential algebras onto the ordinary polynomial algebra, and the intrinsic \(\star\)-bilinear form on \(g\)-polynomials is the pull-back of a single ordinary moment functional \(\mathcal L\). The object of interest is therefore not a new polynomial algebra but the functional generated by the derivator, and our main theorem determines exactly which functionals occur. Let \(c_-\) and \(c_+\) be the increments of the continuous part of \(g\) on the two sides of the centre, and let \(A\) and \(B\) be the multisets of jump sizes to its right and to its left. Then \(\mathcal L\) is Lebesgue measure on \([-c_-,c_+]\), plus an endpoint derivative functional governed by the elementary symmetric functions of \(A\), plus an absolutely continuous left tail whose density is the survival function of a sum of independent exponentials with means in \(B\); the positions of the jumps disappear. Every quadruple \((c_-,c_+,A,B)\) occurs and is recovered from \(\mathcal L\), so the fibres are described exactly, and \(\mathcal L\) is representable by a positive measure precisely when \(|A|\le1\). A weighted lattice extension, in which the transported moments are the factorial moments of the weight, is treated separately.

title: On the Metric Distortion of the Minimum Spanning Tree Problem
abstract: We study the metric distortion of the minimum spanning tree (MST) problem when numerical edge weights are unavailable and each vertex reports only a ranking of the other vertices induced by these weights. We first show, through a simple example, that without assumptions on the weights, no ordinal algorithm guarantees a finite approximation ratio. We therefore focus on general metrics and present a Borůvka-inspired algorithm using only ordinal comparisons that achieves distortion $O(\log n)$. We complement this result by showing that, for every $\varepsilon>0$, no deterministic ordinal algorithm guarantees distortion at most $3/2-\varepsilon$ on all finite metric instances. We then investigate more informative settings in pursuit of constant distortion, first considering two well-studied metric classes. For tree metrics realized on the given vertex set, a more careful variant of our initial algorithm achieves distortion~$1$, recovering an optimal MST from ordinal information alone. For the broad class of doubling metrics, a different algorithm based on \emph{endpoint cut stability} achieves distortion $2^{O(D)}$, where $D$ is the doubling dimension; this is constant for fixed $D$, independently of $n$. Finally, we study a query-based extension allowing comparisons between two edge lengths without revealing their numerical values. For general metrics with $n\geq2$, fewer than $n$ edge-comparison queries suffice to achieve distortion at most $2\log_2^* n-1$, which is near-constant even for very large inputs.

title: Distinguishability and Recovery for a Doubly Sparse Spiked Wigner Model
abstract: We study distinguishability and recovery of a sparse rank-one signal in a spiked Wigner model with independently sparse noise through a variety of algorithms and parameter regimes. The signal and noise have separate sparsity parameters, while the signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) remains of constant order as the matrix size grows. For sub-Gaussian noise and spikes whose nonzero coordinates are bounded away from zero, a leave-one-out quadratic thresholding procedure (a generalization of Ding et al., 2024) identifies the support. Sign synchronization yields exact recovery for a Rademacher spike, and spectral refinement yields strong recovery. The quadratic thresholding search parameter gives an explicit tradeoff between signal sparsity, noise sparsity, and computational cost. We also study extensions to sub-Gaussian spike priors through diagonal and quadratic thresholding. For Rademacher spikes with continuous nonzero noise, we develop an identical search algorithm that exploits unblurred signal entries, the existence of which permits distinguishability; connectivity of the graph they reveal provides a sufficient condition for exact recovery. These guarantees do not require moment assumptions on the continuous noise distribution. Together with our previous PCA results (Dumitriu et al., 2026), our analysis covers almost the entire space of parameters and regimes for distinguishing and recovering in our doubly sparse spiked Wigner model.

title: Permutationally Invariant Polynomial Descriptors as Colored Multigraphs
abstract: The combinatorial explosion in monomial counts limits the extension of global permutationally invariant polynomial (PIP) potential energy surfaces to larger molecular systems. We use graph-theoretic language to reformulate PIPs as colored multigraphs and develop a series of theoretical and computational tools. First, we introduce an offline PIP generation algorithm whose cost has an upper bound independent of atom count for a fixed degree cutoff and number of element types. Second, we introduce a new online PIP evaluation algorithm, termed tensor-network descent. For the full PIP set through degree $d$ in a system of $M$ atoms, the evaluation complexity for $1\le d\le14$ is $O\!\left(f(d)M^{\left\lfloor(\sqrt{1+8d}+1)/2\right\rfloor}\right)$. At the commonly used cutoff of $d=5$, the online evaluation complexity decreases from the $M^{10}$ scaling of conventional explicit term-by-term computation to $M^3$. Numerical tests using the full PIP set through degree 5 show that our method achieves speedups of several orders of magnitude on most MD17 systems and remains computationally affordable for systems containing more than one thousand atoms. The method has a native tensor form, supports automatic differentiation, and provides a unified theoretical construction of four classes of PIP descriptors defined consistently across systems---global, atom-centered, bond-centered, and cluster-centered---establishing a representation and computational foundation for PIP potentials for large systems and for transfer across systems. Together, these results show that PIPs are neither inherently restricted to small systems nor intrinsically nontransferable.

title: VulnSAGE: Adjudicating SAST Reports by Connecting LLM Reasoning to Program Structure
